#6801. Here’s What It Takes to Keep a Pool Running During the Winter, According to Experts

Before you dive in, it’s important to understand the risks and expenses involved.

When most people think of backyard swimming pools, relaxing outdoors in the summertime immediately comes to mind. But some homeowners don’t want the swimming season to end when temperatures drop. Fans of cold-water swimming are starting to consider ways to enjoy their pools throughout the winter as a part of an at-home wellness experience.

“Ten years ago, most people didn’t think winter swims were possible, especially in colder climates,” says Karen Larson, cofounder of Soake Pools. “Times have changed because these days, they’re seeing neighbors, friends, and others do it and post the proof on social media.”

The increasing interest in cold-water experiences is part of a broader wellness trend. In American College of Sports Medicine's 2026 Worldwide Fitness Trends report, cold therapies, including cold plunges, cryotherapy, and cold showers, earned the 17th spot among fitness trends for the year, up from number 20 in its 2025 report.

If you’ve previously closed your swimming pool around Labor Day but are interested in making cold-water swimming a part of your daily wellness routine, there’s a lot to keep in mind. Not every existing pool is a good candidate for keeping open for winter swimming, and it’s important to understand the risks and expenses involved. But if you’re curious, here’s what to consider about keeping a pool open year-round.

Why is cold-water swimming becoming more common? There are numerous purported mental and wellness benefits, from athletic recovery to stress relief and better sleep. A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis published in PLOS ONE found that cold-water immersion led to a reduction in stress for 12 hours afterward as well as improvements in sleep quality and overall quality of life.

“Winter swimming often creates a time where friends and family can come together without distractions,” adds Larson.

That said, while swimming during the colder months has its perks, there are also several risks to keep in mind. A 2020 review in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health found that cold-water immersion can trigger an immediate shock response, leading to involuntary gasping, hyperventilation, and a rapid increase in heart rate and blood pressure. These reactions can make it difficult to control your breathing and increase your risk of drowning. Cold temps can also impair your muscle strength and nerve function, making it challenging to swim safely.

It’s a good idea to acclimate to the cold water gradually and avoid prolonged exposure. You’ll also want to make sure there’s someone else home while you take your cold-water plunge in the pool.

In addition, if you have underlying conditions like heart disease, consult your doctor before all else, as the cold water may place additional strain on your heart.

If you’re trying to consider whether your pool is a good candidate to keep open during the colder months, these are the things to look into.

The cost of keeping a swimming pool open for winter swimming will depend on your location, size, desired water temperature, and the type of heater you use.

“Routine pool maintenance generally remains about the same year-round, although chemical consumption may decrease depending on how frequently the pool is used,” explains Jim Eisch, Jr., vice president of operations at Pinch A Penny Pool Patio Spa. “The biggest expense to consider in the winter is heating the pool.”

For this reason, prospective winter swimmers may want to consider an upgrade to their heating system. Instead of using pricey natural gas heating or a traditional heat pump, Eisch says that inverter technology is one of the most affordable ways to maintain a swimmable pool temperature year-round.

For example, if you live in Florida and have a 10,000-gallon swimming pool, Eisch estimates your annual heating costs will be $2,467 with a natural gas heater, $741 with a traditional heat pump, and $434 for a heat/cool pump that uses inverter technology.

As aforementioned, the goal with wintertime swimming is not to be soaking in bathwater-like temperatures while it’s freezing outside. For safety purposes, winter swims are quick, and the heating system is to keep your chlorinated pool water well above the 19-degree Fahrenheit freezing point.

Unsurprisingly, a standard 14-by-28-foot swimming pool is going to be one of the hardest to use effectively year-round, unless you live in a region with a mild wintertime climate.

“You can technically use a large pool year-round, but it’s difficult to cover all its surface area well enough to hold in the heat, so heating bills can climb fast,” says Larson.

Therefore, smaller sizes like a 10-by-16-foot cocktail pool or plunge pool are better candidates for keeping open. Dedicated winter swimmers should also invest in an easy on-and-off cover—or a motorized auto cover—for added protection.

Regular pool cleaning and maintenance are essential, and this upkeep over the winter is no exception.

“Check the filtration system regularly to make sure it’s circulating smoothly, monitor the water chemistry, and plan for power outages—because there’s a good chance they will happen,” Larson explains. For this reason, you should also invest in a generator that can keep the pump running if the power goes out.

Safe pool access is just as important as any other aspect of the pool’s design. That’s why a nonslip surface, excellent drainage, and ample lighting are key.

“Your design should also provide a clear path from the house to the water,” says Neha Gupta, interior designer and founder at NU Curations.

Especially in the wintertime when ice and snow are a factor in your region, make sure you have a safe and smooth exit plan for getting out of the water, bundled up, and into your warm home without any obstacles. And then, of course, remember to cover the pool back up to keep it protected and ready for your next plunge.

#6799. Everything We Know About The Batman: Part II Thanks to… Heidi Klum?

If you’d told me even a month ago we’d get significant spoilers for The Batman: Part II, the next Robert Pattinson-led Batman movie, in a photo Heidi Klum posted for her annual Halloween costume, I would find that both weirdly specific and entirely unbelievable.

And yet, that looks to be exactly what happened this past weekend when prosthetics supplier The Makeup Armoury posted BTS photos of the work prosthetics expert Mike Marino (who also worked to transform Colin Farrell into The Penguin for the first film and subsequent HBO Max series) was doing for Klum. If you’ve somehow been off-grid for the last few years, you may have missed that the famed supermodel takes Halloween incredibly seriously, frequently donning costumes with extensive makeup and designs that make her unrecognizable. This year was no exception, but it might have gone largely unnoticed had that photo not accidentally revealed clues about the upcoming superhero sequel, which is currently in production with an expected release date of February 18th, 2028.

In the photo, Marino, who provided a helping, ahem, hand in Klum’s costume together for the year, had a number of molds lingering in the background, which have seemingly confirmed that Brian Tyree Henry will play Two-Face, Sebastian Stan will play Victor Zsasz, and that Part II will feature the famed Court of Owls.

Henry’s mold appears to show the Atlanta actor with a disfigured face that mimics the iconic villain. Some, including me, in this very outlet, have, speculated that he might be playing either Dent or Detective Harvey Bullock, a hardened Gotham City cop who frequently works alongside Jim Gordon. But this seems to confirm it. Considering writer-director Matt Reeves has cited Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale’s The Long Halloween as an influence on his version of the Caped Crusader, it’s not ultimately a huge surprise, but perhaps a slight disappointment considering Reeves had stated his intention to move the sequel into uncharted territory by featuring a villain that had “never really been done in a film before.”

Which brings us to Victor Zsasz, who Stan seems to be playing. There was some speculation when he shaved his head upon joining the production he might be playing the character, but the cast looks to confirm the speculation. While the serial killer—who carves tally marks into his body for every person he’s killed—shows up in Batman Begins as a minor enforcer in Carmine Falcone’s crew, he’s got a much larger role in the comic books themselves. In Long Halloween, Zsasz is hired by Falcone to assassinate Dent before he's intercepted by Batman. Might Reeves look to flip the script here and disfigure Henry’s Dent in the process? This interpretation of Zsasz would certainly fit the extremely grounded approach Reeves took in the first installment. But there’s also some confusion here, as Stan was rumored to be playing Harvey when casting first broke and even went so far as to say he’d be playing the role in an interview over the summer. The French publication Le Journal du Dimanche did, however, later retract his statement.

The last accidental spoiler is a big scoop for comic book fans. Simply labeled “Owl 3,” this likely confirms that the Court of Owls will finally make their silver-screen debut. Created in 2012 by writer Scott Snyder and artist Greg Capullo, the Owls are one of the biggest new additions to the Batman canon in recent memory. The Court is a clandestine criminal society made up of Gotham’s wealthiest and most influential citizens, whose power and influence stretch back to the city’s earliest days. They have immeasurable resources and frequently deploy assassins, known as Talons, to do their bidding. This tracks with the story Reeves told in The Batman of a Gotham beset by a history of corruption. Owls are also bats' natural predators; so that, too, is bad news for Battinson.

While this potential leak is exciting and unexpected, it also raises doubts about the identity of Scarlett Johansson’s character, as she was rumored to be playing Harvey’s wife, Gilda Dent. Either way, never in a million lifetimes could we have guessed that Heidi Klum would be the one to spill the beans about one of the most anticipated comic book movies of the next few years.

#6794. The Clarks Wallabee Goes Gorpcore

Clarks has been on one lately. Over the past few weeks, Moncler worked up the British footwear brand's signature Wallabee, while A.P.C. took on the Desert Boot and the Weaver. Now, Clarks has called in Italian shoemaker Diemme to drag three of its biggest silhouettes up a mountain.

(In case you don't spend all day thinking about Italian hiking boots, here's a primer: Diemme was founded in Montebelluna, a town in northern Italy with a very serious footwear-making history. The brand is best known for taking the kinda boots originally built for mountains and making them nice enough to wear with your very best trousers. Every pair is still made at its factory in Veneto, and the upcoming Clarks collection is, too.)

The main event is the Wallabee, of course. Diemme reworked the familiar moccasin-shaped shoe and covered it in pale “champagne” suede from Charles F. Stead, the British tannery responsible for some of the nicest fuzzy leather in footwear. So far, so classic. But then you get the thick rope laces and rubber mudguard wrapped around the bottom. Underneath, the OG crepe sole has been swapped out for the chunky, lugged unit found on Diemme's Roccia Vet and Cornaro boots. It makes the whole shoe sit higher and gives it enough tread to deal with more than a slightly sticky pub floor. Your ’Bees are now ready to hit the trails.

There are two more styles in the cross-branded collection. The Desert Boot comes in the classic “cola” brown suede, only now it's been fitted with a heavy-duty sole. Then there's the Desert Trek, which has been transformed into a mid-cut boot and made from black full-grain leather. It keeps the signature center seam and little Trek Man logo, but it's easily the biggest and baddest of the three, with metal D-rings running up the lacing system and a beefed up ankle for extra support.

The Diemme x Clarks collection is set to drop on November 5, purchasable through Diemme, Clarks, and select stockists globally.

A version of this story originally appeared in British GQ.

The day after the midterm elections, Casey McQuiston, author of Red, White & Royal Blue, is wearing a black bleach tie-dyed shirt with “Texas” on it and joking about “being the main character on the internet—in a good way.”

In their New York Times bestseller, Alex Claremont-Diaz, son of the president of the United States—and boyfriend of Britain’s Prince Henry—orchestrates his Democratic mother’s victory in Texas. It’s a feat the president’s aides mocked him for even proposing and one that gives his mom the electoral college votes she needs to win a second term.

On Tuesday night, as election results showed Democratic candidates James Talarico (for the U.S. Senate from Texas) and Gina Hinojosa (a Texas gubernatorial hopeful) pulling out wins, fans of the book and its movie adaptation began posting memes and references celebrating “Blexas”—Blue Texas, duh—in response.

“Casey McQuiston, this is a WILD marketing budget for the new book & movie but I’m not mad about it,” said one post, a nod to the Red, White and Royal Blue sequel novella, Red, White & Royal Blue: The Private Correspondence, coming out on December 1.

“James Talarico clearly got ahold of Alex Claremont Diaz’s Texas Binder,” said another, referencing the giant file Alex kept his strategy in.

By 11 p.m., Casey had gotten in on the fun, reposting one fan’s meme with the text “keep sending me these i’m bout to bust,” to their Instagram Stories. Two of their favorite mentions came from playwright Jeremy O. Harris and their favorite skincare influencer.

Cosmopolitan talked with Casey less than 24 hours after the Democrats swept Texas about Election Night, predicting a Blue Texas, and what’s next for Alex and Henry.

I was at my sewing machine making some patchwork stuff for Christmas gifts. I had the Steve Kornacki live feed on my computer. I was just passively taking it in, trying not to get too emotionally involved because of what happened in 2024. That was really bad.

At some point, when it was getting close to calling the race for Talarico, I thought, Let’s move this to the living room and lock in, see what’s about to happen. Then I was under my weighted blanket, living for Kornacki. I’ve never seen him so expressive. I didn’t know he was allowed to make faces.

I’m not going to lie, I was walking on sunshine this morning, baby. I couldn’t be happier for Texas and the people I love who live there.

The one thing I’m not is surprised. I knew Texas had this in them all along. It was simply just a matter of having the resources and having the right stars aligning. I’m just so proud of them, and I’m so happy for them.

I’ve been sent so many memes. I generally have a lot of digital boundaries. I don’t look my name up. I stay out of reader spaces, but there are so many memes. I can’t resist.

I don’t think I can even compute that. It’s hard to even conceptualize myself as being part of any canon because when I think of that book, the image that comes to my mind is sitting in my bed at my mom’s house, typing it in Google Docs. It’s still that to me.

I’ve had all these different relationships with it over the 10 years that it’s been in my life. There have been times I found it hard to access the feelings of hope that went into it. There have been times I’ve found it difficult not to want to leave that feeling in the past because of what we’ve been through the last 10 years. It’s so hard to have optimism, and that book is optimistic. What keeps me coming back to it is that I had no idea whether things would get worse or better, but I believed they would get better.

Ultimately, I wrote what I saw: Texas’s heart was a lot more complicated than many people thought, and the people in the state deserve so much better. That’s what I keep coming back to when I think of that back.

First of all, let’s not forget how many fucking electoral votes Texas has. And if you wanted the big moment at the end where you have one state come in and save the election for you, it has to be Texas. It felt like it could be a huge twist, but I could also see it actually happening.

I wanted to do a story where my Democratic president was not a Kennedy but more of a [former Texas State Senator] Wendy Davis or Jimmy Carter. To me, Texas is where you go for that. A few years before, I had watched a livestream of Wendy Davis’s filibuster for abortion rights in Texas. I was so galvanized by that and so amazed to see there was a woman like that who held office in Texas. She really inspired me too, so it just felt right.

Also, in my experience, Texas is the most American of the states. I wanted the juxtaposition of the British aristocracy and the American gunslinger vibe.

No, I haven’t. But I’ve heard there’s a Red White fan on the Talarico campaign or someone who worked closely with them. I don’t blame anyone on any campaign for not necessarily wanting to campaign with a gay smut author before Election Day in a tight race. I’m like, Let’s play it safe. I’ll catch you after your victory lap.

I am hoping I’ll hear from the Talarico campaign. I would love to do a collab.

A lot of people look the other way because they might not have a trans person in their life directly affected by it or they might think there are so few trans athletes that this isn’t a real problem.

I think what we’ve learned from history is that it’s never that simple. It’s almost always boiling the frog in water, slowly raising the temperature to see what they can get away with. We really do have to keep our eye on the ball when it comes to anti-trans legislation, even if it seems frivolous.

1,000 percent. Romance from its inception is deeply political. So much of the early proto-romance was rooted in, Let’s write a how-to guide on how good women should behave so their virtue could be rewarded with true love. Then we had waves of the Austen of it all.

Going back to more recent years, the ’70s or so, so much of it was about centering agency and pleasure and, in some weird ways, even educating about sexuality and what your body can do other than be legislated, abused, and prevailed upon.

Anytime we have a juggernaut sub-industry of media that is predominantly driven by women and marginalized people, and those stories are centered on those people, that is hugely political. So, yes, I don’t think we can ever separate politics from romance. It’s baked into the pie.

Most of Cat Sebastian’s backlist I think of as really political queer romance. They’re not necessarily about politics, but politics are part of the journey we’re on.

When I think of political romance, I also think a lot about Beverly Jenkins. I think we all do. Much of her backlist, especially the stuff she was writing in the ’90s, is super political and fun to read.

They would be in Texas. Alex is hosting the watch party. He’s trying to keep it professional. Until 10 p.m., it was more of passed-apps vibe; after 10 p.m., it became a full-on, slam-down, hoedown fucking party. There was a lot of dancing and some light crowd surfing.

It would be one of those nights where you’re having the most fun celebrating something, and you’re looking at your partner across the room, and you’re locking eyes, and you’re both thinking, It’s on later when we’re alone. Then as soon as you’re alone, you just pass out.

Red, White & Royal Blue: The Private Correspondence is an epistolary novella. The concept is that after their emails were leaked in Red, White & Royal Blue, Alex and Henry swore they would never write emails to each other again. But they still want to write. So this is a collection of all of their handwritten letters, notes, cards, everything else over 20 years after the end of the first book. It covers everything from getting married to moving to Texas to starting a family and Texas electoral politics.

If you have been curious to know what happens to Alex and Henry after the end of the book, I got you. I’ve got 20 years’ worth of answers for you in this novella. It’s really fun. It’s silly, and it’s definitely horny at points and angsty too. But more than anything else, it takes a lot of what I loved from the first book: those emails where they’re really pouring their hearts out to each other, connecting so intimately through words, and letting that cook for you for, you know, 300 pages.

#6792. Will There Be Fewer Gowns at the Met Gala Next Year?

Announced today, the theme of the 2027 exhibition explores fashion’s obsession with everyday garments like T-shirts, jeans, and trench coats

Just over two months ago, the Met Costume Institute canceled its John Galliano retrospective, the original theme for the 2027 exhibition, amid donor and patrons outcry—today, it has announced the new direction, and it’s as far from Galliano’s fantastical fashions as possible.

The 2027 Costume exhibition and corresponding gala is titled “extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday.” It will explore how designers reimagine quotidien ideas for the high-fashion world and how wearing, styling, and caring for these garments shapes their significance over time.

The exhibition will be divided into two larger themes. The first, “Familiar Forms,” will center archetypal garments like jeans, T-shirts, biker jackets, and trench coats, looking at how designers reinvent these pieces and play with the symbolism surrounding them. The other, “Common Matter,” will focus on disposable materials like paper, aluminum, and plastic, and how they have been elevated to fashion.

“The ordinary is never quite as simple as it appears,” said Andrew Bolton, Curator in Charge of the Costume Institute. “A pair of jeans, a white shirt, or a sweatshirt can hold traces of a life—the habits, memories, and attachments that make something our own. Designers work with that familiarity, revealing unexpected possibilities within forms and materials we think we already know. The exhibition invites us to discover how much imagination the everyday can hold, and how looking again might change what we value and care for.”

Bolton began where he left off last year with “Costume Art,” and the reality of placing the body at the center of your design process. He was particularly interested in moments like Jun Takahashi’s fall 2024 collection for Undercover, titled “Watching a Working Woman,” which was inspired in part by Wim Wenders’s 2023 film Perfect Days. He created ensembles that joined and layered familiar garments in new ways to subvert and complicate traditional perceptions of identity and form. The exhibition will open with pieces from this collection and expand to include over 200 items, including Matthieu Blazy’s trompe l’oeil leather jeans for Bottega Veneta, pieces from Marc Jacobs’s 1990s Perry Ellis grunge collection, Brooke Shields’s Calvin Klein jeans, Junya Watanabe’s leather biker jackets, Charles James’s 1930s couture puffer coat, and more.

The original theme, which would have centered on Galliano’s life and work, was initially announced in late July. After donors and critics spoke out against the designer’s past antisemitic and anti-Asian remarks, it was then recalled in late August. This decision was unprecedented; the Met had never made such a late-stage switch-up.

Galliano was known for his objectively extraordinary work subverting themes of historical excess and grandeur. His shows were more like theater productions. Now, it seems they’ve chosen a balm for the raucous in skewing in the complete opposite direction, promoting real life over fantasy. That said, this new theme is purported to examine familiar ideas through the extraordinary lens of fashion. There is certainly nothing ordinary about a Junya Watanabe biker jacket.

There is certainly much to explore here. The theme reminds us how much inspiration comes from the people walking down the street every day, the uniforms that have shaped our perceptions of society. Those ideas are ripe material for fashion designers’ creative minds —and can cause quite the stir among audiences. Just think of how shocked the industry was after Marc Jacobs elevated the way youth culture were dressing, what we call “grunge,” to the runway with his 1993 collection for Perry Ellis. Or the fascination with those optical illusion leather jeans Matthieu Blazy put on his Bottega Veneta runways a few years ago. After all, fashion is only fantastical relative to what we deem commonplace. We need a bit of the the familiar to help us digest something radical.

#6791. The Best Early Black Friday Clothing Deals 2026 Are Here

Before you start questioning your own reality, Black Friday is still a ways away. But it's not too early to start taking advantage of some early Black Friday clothing deals that already sprouting up. Retailers seem more eager than ever to get the sales started early this year, and at this rate, Black Friday will be here before you know it. And some of the hardest-hitting discounts land before the official day even kicks off.

And it’s not just like the stalwarts like Gap, Banana Republic, Abercrombie and J.Crew in the mix, although they are heavily in the mix. Killer indies like Lost & Found and Haven also have a host of discounted goods, and outdoor behemoth REI is feeling especially generous for early November. So, if you’re trying to shop away the daylight savings blues or just feel like getting a jump on holiday shopping, you’re in the right spot.

Abercrombie doesn’t have any specific promotions that are live at the moment, but the sale section was recently stuffed with some ideal fall building blocks—most notably some baggy cords—that will make a refresh as easy and affordable as you’d ever hoped it could be.

Banana Republic has been on a heater recently, and the perfectly-curated Archive Reissue collection is leading the charge this season. It should also be noted that anything on the site that is on sale also gets an additional 20% off.

Don’t tell anyone at Gap that Black Friday is a ways off, because there are a ridiculous number of in-season pieces up to 50%—sweaters, flannels, cords, jeans, jackets, and more—and it feels like raising too much awareness to that might cause some reconsideration and none of us want that.

Haven isn’t promoting a sale anywhere on the site and you might have to dig a little bit depending what size you wear, but if you’re looking for some of the sickest IYKYK brands on the planet at insane discounts, there aren’t many places I’d rather start.

If you’re not familiar with Huckberry, they preside over one of most thoughtfully curated assortments of menswear, footwear and gear anywhere, whether that’s IRL or URL. They haven’t kicked off anything Black Friday specific yet—again, it’s early—but if you haven’t gone through the sale tab in a while, you’re missing out on some preposterously good deals.

Nearly all of J.Crew’s spring-summer collection is on sale at the moment, over 300 pieces up to 40% off through May 26—including a whole bunch of heat-beating shirting, lightweight pants, archive classics and basically anything else you’d want to be on sale.

The first name in denim has a pretty nifty “buy two, get 30% off” promotion going on site-wide, so if you’re searching for some jeans, you might just want to buy a couple pairs. (Or maybe a trucker. Or sherpa-lined trucker. You’re in charge.)

Diving into Lost & Found’s sale section is one of the more enjoyable shopping experiences one can have online right now: the selection is great, the brand list is a top-five worldwide and there’s plenty of inventory, which puts it in stark contrast with some of the less rewarding sale sections.

One of the most quietly great, easy-to-wear brands in the game recently reloaded the sale section, and basically no category was left unturned. Of particular note, are the killer sweatshirts currently available with a healthy discount applied.

Mr Porter’s sale section is the kind you can lose an hour in without realizing it, even months after a seasonal sale has ended. Case in point: there’s roughly 500 pairs of shoes and 900 jackets on sale at this very moment, and while sizes might be hit and miss, the deals aren’t.

REI’s Deals section always lives up to the billing, but right now it’s about as good as it’s ever been. Hundreds of pieces from heavyweights like Arc’teryx, Patagonia, The North Face and more are discounted up to 50%, including plenty of winter-specific gear for anyone lacking in that department.

Todd Snyder presumably won’t be partaking in the Black Friday festivities this year—they announced a new sale structure a while back—but that doesn’t mean the already-on-sale fare doesn’t hold up to the promotions sure to fire up across the board.

This year in the US, Black Friday is on Friday, November 27, a day after Thanksgiving. While that’s the official date, many retailers roll out deals throughout November. You can expect the biggest discounts to happen between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday, but be on the look out for retailers to launch sales early.

Cyber Monday lands on November 30 this year, the Monday after Thanksgiving. Most brands keep the deals rolling through the week—but that doesn't mean a deal will last all day, so act fast.

Are clothing deals better on Black Friday or Cyber Monday?

Black Friday and Cyber Monday both deliver a plethora of clothing deals, but they play a little differently. Big-name retailers and legacy brands usually kick things off on Black Friday, while smaller menswear boutiques tend to hold their fire until Cyber Monday. Expect solid discounts starting around 20% off—and keep your eyes peeled for the coveted sale-on-sale action that’s become the norm in recent years.

#6790. Under the Surface

Canali gives a behind-the-scenes look at sartorial excellence: the time, precision and mastery that transform raw materials into a jacket made to last

Under the surface, unseen layers lie. They stay there, silent. They don’t demand the spotlight. They don’t seek glory. And yet, like a beating heart, they form the innermost foundation of any real achievement. Where passion, enthusiasm, and discipline meet, the logic of excellence takes shape. Such is the story of Under the Surface, the newest creative collaboration from Canali.

Under the Surface is a look at the unseen architecture of a sartorial jacket by Canali. Every Canali jacket is born from a complex system of about 200 steps, each executed with meticulous care. Around 15 specialists are involved in the process—one that sees more than 520 feet of thread sewn into 22,000 stitches, both machine- and hand-made. Unseen when looking at the finished garment, the process informs each piece’s quality, comfort, shape, and durability.

It’s not just a matter of talent: rather, it’s about staying faithful to one’s goals, pursuing them with dedication even when no one is watching. It’s then that quality truly makes a difference, and the end result becomes the visible manifestation of a long creation process that demands great effort, experience and willpower.

That commitment of excellence unites the sartorial world of Canali and Ethan Hawke, the brand’s new Global Ambassador. The actor, writer, and director has dedicated almost four decades to perfecting his art, with endless, ever-learning curiosity. For their new Fall/Winter 2026 campaign, Canali has decided to capture what goes on behind the scenes. In the film, Hawke pores over his scripts, rehearses lines, refines each motion: a painstaking introspective process made of research, study, and exercise, preceding each of his performances.

The behind-the-scenes of a Canali jacket starts with selecting the finest fabrics, sourced from the best Italian wool mills. Then, each textile is examined and interpreted. While technology now allows extreme precision and control, some assessments are still left to the eye and expertise of human specialists. Even tiny details such as slightly different shades of color or variations in texture can influence the final product.

The fabric is then stabilized via steaming cycles and specific treatments, to ensure its behavior remains consistent over time. Then it’s time for digital mapping, guiding every cutting room decision: here, each of the jacket’s pieces is carefully positioned to also help keep waste to a minimum. It’s the first irreversible step.

The garment’s three-dimensional structure is then shaped upon the canvas. Canali crafts theirs in-house, adapting it to each model’s fit and fabrics. Made from horsehair, plant fibers, and natural reinforcements, the canvas is modeled on custom-made concave shapes, known as Schiena d’Asino (Donkey’s Back), which replicate the chest’s anatomy. The canvas is crucial for determining how a jacket drapes over the body, avoiding stiffness. It’s here that the volume of the chest, the balance of the silhouette and ease of wearing begin to be defined.

Then it’s time to craft the front, lapel, padded shoulder, and the sleeves. From planning to execution, nothing’s left to chance. The tailor observes, corrects, iterates. It’s a patient process, requiring time, knowledge, and skill. Lastly, the various layers are united through basting, stitching, and ironing processes. As these details interact, the garment takes on its structure and sophisticated character.

Something special also takes place behind the scenes with Hawke: day after day, the actor’s preparation subtly transforms his thoughts and behavior until, almost by instinct, he takes on each role’s intimate characteristics.

Time underpins the whole process. After being assembled and pressed, the jacket is allowed to rest, to dissipate the steam and stabilize the cloth. This is how the fabric finds its balance, and the garment gains a sort of memory: the ability to naturally find its shape again, even after having been worn, folded, or packed into a suitcase.

In over 90 years of heritage, Canali has refined their techniques through repetition, experience, and experimentation. Each garment is built upon the time-tested values of care, know-how, precision. The Canali style is not one made of grand gestures, but daily practice, intimate and subtle: the constant research into a shape that lasts. One hero of the Under the Surface project is the vicuña jacket, available exclusively at selected flagship boutiques by Canali.The campaign, and the collaboration between Canali and Ethan Hawke, speak to the art of shaping oneself, guided by an ambition to do things well with patience and self-awareness. Both in tailoring and in cinema, there is so much quiet work that happens behind the scenes to make creativity possible. Discipline and rigour do not constrain creative freedom; they make it possible. For Canali, excellence takes shape through the craftsmanship with which each element is made. For Ethan Hawke, it is the preparation that allows him to approach each role with confidence.And, as the Under The Surface campaign reveals, each of these steps adds something essential to the finished product. In the case of the Canali cashmere and vicuña blazer (the hero style of the FW26 campaign), it is structure, movement, character, durability, and a lightness that can only be achieved through the combination of expertly-chosen materials and complex fine tailoring. The knowledge required to execute this is almost tangible, felt in the quality of the piece.

The finished result only has value because of the strong, unseen structure underneath. It is a story we can all resonate with. Little by little, layer by layer, day by day, we each build ourselves in pursuit of excellence. Our actions create the people we are – even, or especially, when nobody is watching – in the same way that the apparent simplicity of a piece of clothing hides the depth of work required to craft it. This is the essence of Under the Surface.

#6789. Meet Levi Alves McConaughey: Matthew McConaughey and Camila Alves’s Son

The 18-year-old is stepping into the spotlight

Is Levi Alves McConaughey Hollywood’s next rising star to know? Matthew McConaughey and Camila Alves’s eldest son turned 18 earlier this year and seems to be following in his father’s footsteps, gradually stepping into his own spotlight.

Over the years, Levi has joined his famous parents on red carpets and at industry events, most recently at last night’s Airbnb.Org Gala in Los Angeles, where he even had his own solo moment on the red carpet. With two acting credits, a runway debut, and several Fashion Week appearances under his belt, he’s beginning to build a public persona of his own. And in the world of celebrity offspring, all signs certainly point to a career in the making for Levi.

Here’s everything to know about the young McConaughey, who’s just getting started.

Matthew McConaughey and Camila Alves McConaughey welcomed their first child, Levi Alves McConaughey, on July 7, 2008. He’s the eldest of the Hollywood couple’s three children. They also share a daughter, Vida (born in 2010), and a son, Livingston (born in 2012).

Over the years, Matthew has spoken about the importance of instilling a strong work ethic in his three children. During a 2020 appearance at The History Channel’s HISTORYTalks, the actor called his kids his “living legacy” and said he taught them the value of hard work by giving them small jobs on his sets.

“I have my kids come out, we put them to work,” the Dazed and Confused star said. “We give them a little cash for catering.”

Levi has also joined his parents in giving back. In 2023, Alves brought Levi and daughter Vida to Refettorio Paris, where they helped cook and serve meals to people in need. Levi later reflected on the experience in an Instagram post, writing, “I got the chance to cook at @refettorioparis for some people that don’t normally get to have a really nice meal. Refettorio Paris serves first class meals to the homeless. They made a great restaurant with high-end chefs to cook—using produce that was going to be thrown away.”

He added, “It was really cool to serve some people that don’t normally get to have it.”

Levi made his acting debut in the 2025 film The Lost Bus, starring opposite his father. The up-and-coming actor plays Shaun McKay, the son of Kevin McKay, who is portrayed by his real-life dad.

But as he tried out for the role. Levi didn’t want his famous last name to give him a leg up. In an interview with People, the father-son duo revealed that Levi auditioned for the role anonymously, with his last name removed so he could earn the part all on his own.

“Can you pull the last name?” Matthew asked the film’s casting director. “She goes, ‘Yeah.’ And I got a call back and she said, ‘Our director Paul Greengrass said, ‘That’s the kid. That’s the son, Levi.’ And then she goes, and ‘I told him that’s actually Matthew’s son in real life.’”

For Levi, the role was an opportunity to explore his interest in acting. “This role wasn’t me going, ‘Oh, I’m going to become an actor,’ It was me saying, ‘I’m really interested in this.’”

Levi has entered the fashion scene on a few occasions, including sitting front row at the Dior Homme Spring 2026 show during Paris Fashion Week.

He also made his official catwalk debut during Milan Fashion Week this season, walking the Vogue World runway.

In 2025, Levi opened up to Interview magazine about his mom, dad, and budding Hollywood career. The teen shared why he idolizes both of his parents: “My dad for the man he is, because of the work he has been able to create, and how he’s handled it all,” he said. “My mom for the woman she is, her patience, and her want to help others.”

When asked if he wanted to be famous, he said, “Famous in a lasting way. I want to continue to build on a legacy that I have the privilege to carry on.”

#6788. Anne Hathaway and J.Lo Both Love Chocolate Cherry Nails: Here’s How to Wear Them This Fall

The chocolate-brown-meets-cherry-red combo is entirely irresistible.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

At this point, I know all too well that my fall manicure rotation will always include some variation of burgundy nails, chocolate brown nails, and black cherry nails. But what happens when you combine all three? You get chocolate cherry nails, the rich, red-meets-brown manicure that’s been getting a lot of love from Hollywood. Jennifer Lopez has given the moody shade her stamp of approval and Anne Hathaway stepped out wearing a similar cherry cocoa manicure earlier this year.

“Chocolate cherry is one of those wonderfully safe, sophisticated colors that simply goes with everything,” says nail artist Max Estrada. “It’s versatile enough to complement almost any wardrobe, which is precisely why I think celebrities gravitate towards it. It’s glamorous without demanding too much attention, but it certainly knows how to make an entrance.” From short, glossy nails à la Anne Hathaway to longer, dramatic tips inspired by J.Lo, chocolate cherry is proof that sometimes the coolest manicure trends are the simplest ones. Ahead, everything you need to know about getting the look, plus inspiration for your next nail appointment.

Chocolate cherry is the marriage of two fall nail colors: deep cherry red and chocolate brown. Unlike a traditional burgundy, which is more of a winey purple, chocolate cherry is a warmer with a brown undertone. (And it’s pretty dang expensive-looking, I might add.) “It’s incredibly easy to wear without being boring,” says Estrada. “You get the classic elegance of a red manicure mixed with the richness of chocolate brown, creating something that feels expensive, polished and a little mysterious.”

The color is also a perfect transitional shade for fall and winter manicures. As the weather cools off, “we naturally move away from the bright, playful colors of summer towards deeper, warmer tones,” says Estrada. “Chocolate cherry captures that transition perfectly. It has the romance of a deep red and the warmth of autumnal brown, making it an incredibly flattering seasonal color.”

The color looks gorgeous as a simple, solid-color manicure, but there’s also plenty of room to play around with different nail shapes, finishes, and designs. “Personally, I adore a beautifully tapered, long almond nail in chocolate cherry,” says Estrada. “There’s something incredibly vampy, sensual, and sophisticated about that silhouette, especially with an ultra-glossy finish.” He also likes the color with a square nail too.

If you want to get into some nail art, you can go simple or get adventurous with it: “I would also love chocolate cherry with a magnetic velvet cat-eye effect, creating that gorgeous multidimensional movement in the color,” Estrada says. “Or imagine a deep chocolate base with an exaggerated cherry-red French tip.”

Nail prep is always key to a professional-looking mani, especially when you’re working with darker polish, which can be less forgiving. If you’re doing a DIY manicure and you don’t know where to start, here are some tips from Estrada. First, push back your cuticles. “I always recommend gently pushing back the cuticle area, carefully removing excess dead cuticle tissue, refining the nail shape and ensuring every nail looks consistent,” he says.

Next, before applying polish, make sure your nails are clean and dry. “The nail plate should be properly cleansed and prepared before application, while the surrounding skin should be kept beautifully conditioned,” he adds. “Proper preparation means better adhesion, longer wear and a much more luxurious-looking manicure.”

Next, an insider tip: “One of my favorite professional techniques is leaving the tiniest clean margin between the polish and the surrounding skin,” he says. This way your polish is less likely to bleed onto the edges of your finger, which can look messy.

After you’ve applied the polish, he recommends finishing with a cuticle oil for hydration.

#6786. Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman Is the Scariest Thing You’ll See All Year

In 2009, Andrew Garfield found a thread. He was preparing to play Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg in a little-hyped film called The Social Network, and he had located the thing in Zuckerberg’s story that he could pull on—the through line that turns personal experience into empathic performance and on into universal storytelling. Then he lost the part to Jesse Eisenberg. Director David Fincher had seen what, today, is obvious: Humanity flows fast and deep through Andrew Garfield. Fincher cast him instead as Eduardo Saverin, the betrayed cofounder and emotional counterweight to Zuckerberg’s opacity, who cries, sneers, throws a feint, and smashes a laptop (that’s one scene).

The movie made him a celebrity, and he brought an unusual depth of emotion to this job too. While serving as Spider-Man, he begged the public, via a handwritten sign held up for paparazzi, to care about a more important cause than what’s up with famous people. While promoting 2021’s Tick, Tick…Boom! on The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, he talked about the death of his mother; the clip still gets shared by grieving people.

Boxers by Hermès. Sneakers by Bottega Veneta. Socks by Jacques. Watch by Rolex.

Now, 15 years after The Social Network, Garfield has picked back up the tech-CEO thread to play Sam Altman in Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s film that covers the founding of OpenAI up to the coup that led to Altman’s firing—and his re-entrenchment. (OpenAI has an agreement with Condé Nast, the owner of GQ, which allows OpenAI to display its content in search results for a limited term.) The movie seems destined to occupy the same orienting role as The Social Network, helping us understand the technology and the men who are shaping our futures, almost in real time. But whereas that film was a legal drama about status (Harvard guy vs. hotter, richer-born Harvard guys), Artificial plays as a horror movie where the monster, AI, is real. (And it just learned how to do theoretical physics.)

Garfield brings Altman to life as a mad guidance counselor: rubbing the shoulders of engineers, taking security meetings cross-legged, and sucking green juice in the faces of his adversaries. Here, finally, is an ascendant tech overlord that makes unsettling use of Garfield’s famous sensitivity. When Garfield-as-Altman cries, you’re not sure whether they’re the tears of a true superintelligence believer or a duplicitous power-seeker. Or which one would be scarier.

When we meet in early October, Garfield is transformed by a beard and shoulder-length hair. He grew it all out to play the magician Roy Horn, of Siegfried and Roy, in next year’s show Wild Things, though they ended up putting a wig on him anyway. He was filming that limited series in Berlin immediately after wrapping The Uprising, a Paul Greengrass movie about the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, which shot before Artificial was even technically wrapped. “I did these three things back to back last year, and I did have a bit of burnout, to be honest. I was kind of sleepless in Berlin for a while, and not in a romantic way,” he says. “It was rough, dude. I should have just gone to Berghain and just rode it out.” Now, though, Garfield is visibly buzzing, both from watching Artificial with an audience at the New York Film Festival the night before—and from the chatter coming out of Silicon Valley.

This interview has been condensed and edited.

Andrew Garfield: I’ve listened to his podcast.

The walk was a key for me, and the clothes and the physicality. He’s a very slight, slim guy, Sam, and seems to be very image-conscious. Which is interesting to me, which is something that I felt compelled by. There’s a great video of Sam, in what looks like a diner, when he’s talking about Loopt [the company he cofounded before running Y Combinator and cofounding OpenAI], when he’s in his early 20s, and he was much freer with his physicality back then.

Sam did an interview with Vanity Fair [for the magazine’s New Establishment issue]. I think it came out yesterday, the day of our premiere, where he was very sweet about the walk as well. It’s a very generous thing for the boys to acknowledge that the walk was close, a good approximation of Sam and his vibe. I think that’s a very classy thing, to acknowledge the thing that seems to be working. But who knows what’s happening in their hearts and minds right now or within the family? I can project myself into that experience and imagine what it must feel like for an actor to be so presumptuous to play a character called Sam Altman in a major film. I can imagine that must be really strange, and I feel for…. I don’t know. In terms of taking it on, what outweighed that sense of responsibility for me was this sense of it is the defining inevitable invention of our times. It felt like a great responsibility to interrogate not just the machine, if you can even call it that, the kind of the consciousness or the technology itself, but to interrogate the people who are building it and who are putting their hearts and souls and life’s work into it, and where they may or may not be leading us.

That was deeply researched. This is what I gleaned. There’s a lot of people that know Sam. There’s a lot of people that are happy to talk about Sam. Some very, very protective; others, slightly more inside information. And I’m not going to name who these people are. But it was a kind of adding to the cauldron and through my lens of the interpretation of who this person is, combined with what was on the page and the specific cinematic story we’re telling and how we’re telling it, and Luca’s tastes and sensibilities. And, yeah, a lot of people said he would never sit conventionally. He was always sitting like a little boy.

Intimacy, but also ownership of a space—a kind of subtle, very soft dominance of a space. But also, as you say, a kind of, “Hey, we’re all just hanging out doing the coolest job ever. So why can’t we just sit like we’re in a dorm room?” It’s very psychologically interesting to me and smart. And who knows if it’s all calculated? Who knows if it’s not? I don’t know. What was interesting, in tracking his physicality in all the videos I saw is, at the beginning, he’s very free in how he twitches and moves. He’s just freer in his ability to be his true self maybe. And then as he starts to become more and more powerful, and ultimately becoming the face of the new world, this behemoth company that’s going to define where we are going—even if he doesn’t know where we are going, and none of them do—he becomes a slightly more homogenized version of a tech CEO. That was a really, really interesting kind of journey. And you can see, now, in [Altman’s recent interview with Vanity Fair], he’s very image-conscious, and I am too. I think we all are.

I mean, yes. One has to. This is the job. And this is why I wanted to do it: Because with The Social Network, I was getting ready to play Mark Zuckerberg, and then David Fincher calls me in and says, “We found someone that is just going to do it better. It’s Jesse, but we think you could also play this part. And you’re a very emotional actor, Andrew, so why would we waste all of that on someone who doesn’t seem to feel many emotions?” So Eduardo became my kind of guy, and I was very happy with that. But it left a little dangling thread, and I was like, “I need to understand.” Because I started to explore what it takes to win, to win on that level.

I think I’m a competitive person. I’m an athlete. I was raised by a swimming-coach father and, at that time, a proud capitalist. My dad has evolved his view of the world over the course of the last decades, which I find very moving and touching, as I have evolved my view of winning and losing and the beauty of losing and how humility is the only thing that actually grows us. It’s fucking awful. I hate losing.

No. It’s so much easier. Because you’re on this fucking false pedestal and it’s so much easier for the shit to get kicked out. It’s like, Oh, wait a minute. #6785. My Holiday Wish List Includes One Brand Only

It’s that time of year—when I start dropping not-so-subtle hints to my family and friends about what I want for the holidays. This season, there’s only one thing on my radar—and it comes in a little white box.

Some people think fashion editors are difficult to shop for, because we have extremely singular tastes. While it sometimes rings true that I can be a little particular, there is one fail-safe holiday gift I’m always happy to receive: Pandora jewelry. A charm, a bracelet, a ring, or a chain—personally, I’m open to any, and all, of the above (just in case anyone was wondering).

The holiday wish list practically writes itself, but to give my nearest and dearest a helping hand, I’ve spelled out exactly what each of them could give me below.

We both know I have exquisite taste in jewelry. What can I say? I inherited it from you. With this stackable diamond ring, I’ll carry that fact with me through all of life’s biggest moments. And with any luck, I’ll finally stop stealing from your jewelry box.

Consider this your reminder that Mom isn’t the only woman in your life who delights in a nice piece of jewelry. This Cuban Chain Necklace is as “Timeless” as you are—and as pretty as I am. It’s the perfect Christmas gift for a father to give his daughter.

You make every holiday more special, and when we’re together, that’s the only gift I need. That being said, I wouldn’t refuse a sparkly little memento commemorating our time together. Buy me something nice and I promise I’ll wear it for our next date night.

When I look back on the most magical holidays of my life, I don’t think of the gifts I opened or the food I ate. I think of you, and the joy on your face as you opened the present I chose for you. The best part of my Christmas is always being your Santa.

Remember when we were in elementary school, wearing our matching BFF necklaces? All these years later, our taste in jewelry has evolved, but one thing remains the same: our love for each other. Let’s upgrade the nostalgic symbol with diamonds this time.

#6783. WNBA Finals MVP Gabby Williams on Game 7, Trans Athletes, and Her Cat, Halle Berry

“Print this,” said Joe Lacob, the billionaire owner of the Golden State Valkyries, at the start of the team’s playoff run. “Gabby Williams is the best player in the world."

It was one of the coldest quotes in recent sports memory. But at the time, Williams, the 30-year-old French-American wing, hadn’t yet won a WNBA Championship, much less been named Finals MVP. And, truth be told, no one expected this from the Valkyries, an expansion franchise in only its second year of existence, and one without a single All-WNBA selection on its roster.

No matter. After defeating the Atlanta Dream in a winner-takes-all Game 7 (the first in WNBA history) this past weekend, the Valkyries brought their first ever WNBA Trophy back to the Bay. And it was largely because of Williams, who lived up to Lacob’s promise by executing the most memorable second-half takeover in WNBA Finals history.

Here’s how it went down: With three minutes left in the third, the Valks trailing by six, Williams called for the ball, went between-the-legs, and took a step back jumper from beyond the perimeter. She followed that up moments later with a catch-and-shoot three in Angel Reese’s grill. The following possession, Williams freed herself up from a double team, then sprinted out past the three-point line for a money ball.

Williams’ back-to-back-to-back triples broke Atlanta and gave life to “Ballhalla,” San Francisco’s fortress of 18,064 violet-clad, women’s basketball fanatics. After trailing for most of the game, Golden State snatched the lead and didn’t look back. Williams finished with 28 points in the second half (a WNBA post-season record) on her way to a game-high 30. When it came time to name the Finals MVP, there was little question about which player on an otherwise balanced roster had been most crucial to the Valkyries’ fairytale fun.

Watching Williams, you might not have guessed that, when she’s not hooping, she simply wants to cuddle with her cat and binge-watch anime. Just before the Valks’ championship parade, GQ got to know this smooth assassin a bit more intimately.

I played so bad.” Or “Oh, HB, we won. And this happened.” First thing I do [after winning the WNBA Finals], “HB, we freaking won. Can you believe it?” And she was like, “Can you feed me?”

And she's definitely a Velcro cat. She sleeps right here [next to my face] and there's just no better feeling.

The head of the DOJ’s civil-rights division resigned Thursday. But not to worry. I suspect we’ll see her again—in a congressional hearing room.

I have to admit, “dramatic overhaul” is an interesting way to spell “gutting the division’s actual purpose,” but we move on. Dhillon was an exemplary lemon foisted on the American people by all the lemons above her in the administration. And she was everything they could have wanted.

#6781. In Brooklyn, an Intimate Diwali Dinner Party Bridging Two Easts

On a Sunday night, the elevator doors open onto Rachel Gurjar’s Brooklyn living room. Amaranthus blooms brush brass family heirlooms and fresh pomegranates on a credenza. A tiffin bearing a relative’s initials rests on draped brown fabric. The room could be a still from Gurjar’s debut cookbook, East to East: Recipes and Stories From Mumbai to New York, released October 13.

Barefoot in a pre-draped blue floral sari, Gurjar moves unhurriedly, labelling plates with scraps of tape. She then pulls a white platter from an immaculately organized glass cabinet. “I think this is for the duck,” she says, already moving on.

Since 2021, Gurjar, who grew up in Mumbai, has thrown New York Diwali parties that have acquired a certain lore. One year, she led magazine editors in choreographed Bollywood dances; another, a pani puri fountain presided over a party for 140, with handmade naan to match. “I didn’t have a place to celebrate Diwali myself, so I decided to throw these parties,” she says.

Tonight, the sixth annual gathering is quieter, and intentionally so: a dozen chefs, artists, and designers who helped bring the book to life, on the page or in spirit. If the official launch party was for the public, this one is for her people.

Diwali, the South Asian festival of lights, is widely associated with the triumph of good over evil. It is also an occasion to gather, feed one another, and take stock. Gurjar’s chosen family spans disciplines, with an emphasis on the Black, Brown, and AAPI creatives whose work, she believes, makes New York what it is. “I wanted to make sure that every person at the table had a medium through which they expressed their creativity,” she explains.

Guests include collaborators like designer Ivan Lam of Tender Touch Studios, who picked up flowers that morning; food stylist Sean Dooley, who styled the book’s visuals; and photographer Isa Zapata, a former Bon Appétit colleague who photographed it in Mumbai.

The evening begins with an actually spicy pani puri mezcalita and masala popcorn. Whipped masala and curry leaf butters sit in vintage coupes beside a sweet-sour pomegranate Chex Mix that took Gurjar 12 attempts to perfect. Bollywood music plays as guests pass around bindis and apply them to one another.

The menu moves between Mumbai and New York, yet feels unmistakably familial. Gurjar’s mother, Ranjana, brought potato and rice chips she made in India, sneaking them past TSA. She also spent the week helping her daughter prepare, kneading dough and frying gulab jamun.

“At her core, Rachel is a nurturer,” says chef Josh Osamor, who calls her goat curry one of the most delicious things he has eaten. The two recently collaborated on a Nigerian-Indian supper club. “The biryani jollof was a no-brainer. It was a perfect dance,” he says.

Leanne Gan, an art director at the ACLU, has attended Gurjar’s Diwali parties since the beginning. Adjusting her sea-green dupatta, she dips a rice chip into the Penang curry crab dip. “Rachel is someone who doesn’t settle for less,” Gan says. “It’s been amazing to see her put 110% of herself into these recipes.”

The room erupts with oohs and aahs as artist and fashion designer Misha Japanwala arrives in a gold-and-silver lamé sari and a custom silver breastplate she made using body casting, the same process she used for pieces for Cardi B and Lizzo. (Most recently, Lupita Nyong’o wore Japanwala’s work in The Odyssey.)

“I just felt like I was missing a silver breastplate in my wardrobe, and everybody needs a silver breastplate,” she jokes. She accessorizes with nipple-cast rings and silver jewelry from Karachi, her hometown.

“One of the most beautiful things about moving to New York has been expanding my South Asian circle and being able to celebrate each other in this way,” Japanwala reflects. When she hosted Eid at home for the first time last year, she invited friends from her wider South Asian circle, beyond Muslim Pakistanis. “It really was the most miraculous thing,” she adds. Next to her, fashion designer Sheena Sood of Abacaxi is wearing a mirrorwork lehenga with a matching knit shrug from a 2021 collection.

The contagious joys of Diwali extend beyond the subcontinent: For Manouska Jeantus, founder of the social events company Nous Love Club, the gathering recalls celebrating Haitian Independence Day with her family, even as she eats malai shrimp instead of the soup joumou she grew up with.

Guests take their seats, and Gurjar raises a dirty chai espresso martini for a quick toast. Dinner is a greatest-hits collection from East to East, starting with achari melon salad with tempered pickling spices and garam masala roasted squash slicked with brown butter and lime. Back in the kitchen, Gurjar works two cast-iron skillets at once, searing scored duck breasts for her paanch phoran duck—a crowd favorite—and finishing them with raspberry chimichurri. Platters of rice arrive with naan she and her mother made that morning.

Dessert brings homemade gulab jamun and cardamom sticky toffee cake, which Gurjar floods with caramel and finishes with flaky salt. Osamor shakes up another round of dirty chai espresso martinis. A little dancing gives way to conversation on the couch about the week ahead. It is, after all, a school night, and everyone is pleasantly overfed.

The meal mirrors the book’s central idea: a refusal to draw a neat line between East and West. East to East also makes room for what a cooking reel can leave out: the distance from home, building a career abroad, and watching parents grow older from afar, and other complexities that extend beyond homesickness.

In a rare chapter titled “Cultural Appropriation: Who Really Pays,” Gurjar asks who really benefits when food travels, and who gets left behind. It’s a question she and her creative peers have long discussed. To her, celebrating food’s ability to connect people also means asking who gets to tell its stories.

When I first met Gurjar two years ago at a party, I told her she’d taught me to make perfect short ribs, her Thai-inflected coconut braise. What I didn’t tell her was how rare it felt to see another Indian immigrant pursue a creative path, or how brave I thought she was. She has become that person for others, too, inspiring adventurous cooking and a willingness to take up space.

Some had made a career like hers seem out of reach. “I had experiences where people made me feel it wasn’t an option for me,” Gurjar laments. “Brown people, we’re often scared to dream big because we’ve never been permitted to. And I’m in a phase of life when I’m not saying no to anything.”

Asked about the highlight of her career, Gurjar doesn’t have to look backward. She sips her chai espresso martini and says, “I think I’m living it right now.”

#6780. Three New Fragrances That Guarantee “You Smell Good” Compliments

Contrapposto is the latest brainchild of a beauty industry hitmaker

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

You know when someone smells so good it stops you in your tracks? I ran into a friend recently and spent our entire conversation trying not to make it obvious how distracted her scent made me. Part of the intrigue was that I couldn’t quite place what I was smelling. It was unmistakably floral, but its elusiveness made it all the more magnetic. She was wearing Melting Flowers by Contrapposto.

In sculpture, contrapposto describes the shift in a figure’s weight that gives the body a sense of natural movement. Italian for “counterpoise,” it’s also the name of Nécessaire, Homecourt, and Into the Gloss co-founder and former Elle and WWD editor Nick Axelrod-Welk’s latest venture.

Founded with his husband, Casey Welk, in 2023, Contrapposto began as an aesthetic dermatology practice in West Hollywood and has since expanded into fine fragrance, with its first collection launching this fall. On the surface, the aesthetics and scent might seem worlds apart. But as Nick explains in our conversation ahead, the move reflects a deliberate vision for what he wants Contrapposto to become.

What really connected the clinic and the product for me was this idea of enhancing rather than transforming: enhancing your skin, the way you smell, and the way you feel, rather than turning you into someone else. That became kind of the battle cry for the brand.

I also loved the challenge of fragrance. It's such a subjective category. There's no before and after, no claims. Either you like it, or you don't. And I saw a white space in luxury fragrance, where the more you spend, the more you're expected to project and have people notice your scent. I wanted to do something different.

I wanted to introduce scents that melt into your skin and enhance the way you smell and feel. Because I think the only reason to put something into the world in 2026 is to truly add pleasure to someone’s life.

They’re really meant to be experienced on skin. All of the fragrances are quite heavy in musks and lactones, which are molecules that are very dynamic on skin, so the fragrances come alive when you wear them. They can smell different from what you might expect on paper, too. Someone might think they’d never wear a floral fragrance, for example, but then try Melting Flowers and discover this creamy, addictive, woody, sandalwood base that makes them reconsider.

I wouldn’t call them subtle skin scents, though. These are big fragrances that project. They just have this ability to impart a coziness that I love in all my fragrances.

I approach everything by asking, “Who are the best people in this field?” When I started thinking about creating fragrance, I took a step back and thought about the launches that had made a real impact on me when I was an editor. The one I still think about is Tom Ford Private Blend. I remember seeing it at Barneys or Bergdorf Goodman in New York. The amber bottles and the olfactive profiles. These dark woods, ouds, and leathers were new to a Western audience at the time, and yet there was something inherently addictive and commercial about the scents. They were likable.

That was the balance I wanted to strike with Contrapposto: something new and unique that doesn’t smell like anything else, but also has this inherent commerciality to it—something so appealing that it invites as many people to the party as possible.

I knew fragrance was its own world, with its own language, and that if I wasn’t the expert, I needed to find the expert. My job was to find the right people and get them excited about what I was trying to create, so we could do it together. This led me to Karyn Khoury, who had been instrumental in developing Private Blend during her time at Estée Lauder. But Karyn had retired in 2019, moved to Florida, and wasn’t exactly looking to be found.

Long story short, I was able to reach her through a mutual connection, and over the course of a year, we slowly got to know each other. I had her smell what I had been working on and eventually convinced her to become an advisor for me.

Karyn also introduced me to Shyamala Maisondieu [a master perfumer at Givaudan], and we immediately clicked. She’s the kind of person who lives with the fragrances she’s creating. She wears them on her own skin and pays attention to how they evolve. While developing Musc Pétille, she texted me from vacation to say it was finally complete because someone stopped her to ask what she was wearing.

I knew Frank from interviewing him for my podcast, Eyewitness Beauty, several years earlier. What I quickly realized is that getting a meeting with these master perfumers is one thing, but getting them genuinely excited about what you’re doing is a much bigger challenge.

There are only so many people at his level, and major fragrance houses have very little bandwidth for smaller, independent brands like mine. Any time someone like Frank spends working on Contrapposto is time he isn’t spending on a major client like Calvin Klein or L’Oréal.

Frank is a genius who is well-known for his woody, spicy scents, so I wanted to challenge him to create a floral. I think I was able to entice him by giving him full creative freedom from the start. I told him to create without budget constraints and see how he could bring his signature DNA into a more traditionally floral fragrance, which ended up becoming Melting Flowers, the first fragrance we finished in the line.

I think trends are really fun, and I love following them. I’m obsessed with TikTok trends, beauty trends, all of it. But I think longevity always comes down to having the best product. If you have the best product, you’ll keep a consumer. Loyalty is made with product, not with brand.

We’ve seen plenty of examples of brands that have spiked and then fallen out of favor because a new, fun, shiny thing comes along. With some products, like Nécessaire’s body wash, I think they create an enormous amount of loyalty because nothing beats it. I still buy it with my own money because I just think it’s the best.

I believe in creating things that are a pleasure to use, so you enjoy the process. They should have some sort of immediate benefit, whether it’s an immediate glow from oxygenation, a cap that clicks in an oddly satisfying way, or the experience of feeling and smelling a product—how it makes your shower smell or how it makes your sweaters smell. Those are the things that keep someone coming back and, I think, make a product timeless.

#6779. An Everyman’s Guide to Wearing a Necklace

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

You already have a watch you like. This is the next step in your jewelry journey.

Men’s jewelry, I’ve learned, can be a slippery slope. I’ve been a watch guy since elementary school, if we’re generous enough to count a dual-sided compass/watch on a carabiner as a watch. In college I added a bracelet. I’ve been a ring guy for over ten years, thanks mostly to being married and partially to getting lunch drunk in Albuquerque, going ring shopping for my wife, and finding a sterling silver bear signet ring that I’ve worn nonstop since. I’ve had an earring for two years, thanks to a quick weekend in Miami and a well-timed Harrison Ford interview clip crossing my algorithm about getting his ear pierced in a Claire’s.

Recently, I’ve been curious about my personal final frontier of men’s jewelry—the necklace. The other listings above are all fairly low entry points, safe experiments in the world of men’s jewelry. The earring may be the exception, but this is 2026; one small silver hoop isn’t that daring, even in the Midwest. A necklace has never really been my thing. I haven’t felt the pull. That is, until this year.

For an unrelated project, I was breaking down some of the signature stylistic calling cards of Robert Redford. And there it was, across paparazzi pictures and movie stills and in memoriam roundups. In almost every photo, Redford has some kind of necklace, usually peeking from a precariously unbuttoned western shirt.

Further study of what we can safely call Hollywood’s golden age of off-duty style shows the same: McQueen and Newman and their contemporaries, swanning around on and off film, always wearing some sort of necklace or chain or pendant.

This is, of course, a common trap: to look at a famously handsome Hollywood star and think, yeah, all that’s separating me from THAT is a necklace. And sure, a good cheekbone and clavicle will get you pretty far in life. There’s no magic amulet here, nothing that will shazam you into leading-man looks. But there are a few lessons on styling from guys whose literal job it was to present themselves favorably to the world. And a few lessons on what necklaces to choose to help get there.

So, I put my professional online shopping style writing gig into overdrive, going deep into the Getty Images archives and confusing Google’s settings by repeatedly searching “Insert Hollywood Icon + shirtless” to glean some jewelry 101 tips from the professionals.

Instagram and (theoretically, since I don’t indulge) TikTok are full of maximalizing style trend chasers. Why wear one necklace when you can wear four? Why two rings when each finger could have two rings on it? Why dip your toes in the water when you can cannonball into the deep end? And sure, there’s some je ne sais quoi about just committing to something fully and completely out of the gate. But there’s also a lot of try-hard to it.

We’re channeling a more reserved, less #sponsoredpost era of dressing here that cares less about link clicks and more about how things look in the real world. So start simple and start with a chain. My favorite, and currently on daily rotation, is the Curb Chain from L.A.-based Bloedstone. Mine is sterling silver and in the inch length, which hits closer to the sternum than the neck. That’s the prescribed Hollywood A-lister way to wear it, but chart your own path if you want to. Miansai has a thicker 2mm Cuban chain that’s great too. And while we’re covering the M’s, Mejuri has one too. To my slight surprise, my home state watchmaker Shinola makes one, and less surprisingly so, Esquire-approved David Yurman has this giant one featuring a marketing campaign with Michael B. Jordan, who is picking up McQueen’s (and subsequently Brosnan’s) torch by adapting The Thomas Crown Affair.

There’s a whole vocabulary on link types and thickness and clasps out there. Don’t worry about that for now. Find something that calls to you and click add to cart. We’re starting slowly here.

Parting note. There are a lot of chains worn over T-shirts these days. To each their own, but the leading man’s move is to keep it under your shirt. If you want to show it off, just ditch the buttons.

A chain is simple, and sure, the greats wore them. But more often than not, they had something dangling from that chain. Medallion, pendant, a bottle opener in Cool Hand Luke. McQueen was often photographed, including in the pages of Esquire, wearing a St. Christopher medallion. Seeing as he’s the patron saint of travelers, St. Christopher medallions are having a bit of a cultural resurgence, partially because of their traditional association as a good-luck charm for travelers. There are some fun enamel ones on eBay, including these surfing-specific ones. Every once in a while, Nashville-based Americana experts Imogene + Willie will pull together a vintage edit of St. Christopher medallions that always sell out in around 24 hours. Speaking of Nashville, if you’re going to go new, go with Yearly Co. The gold jewelry experts have a 14k version of the iconography with a pitch-perfect 24-inch chain. I can attest to the quality—I gave my wife the brand’s diamond huggies and she wears them almost every day. As the grandson of a Protestant minister, I steer away from the saints out of genetic loyalty to Luther’s 95 Theses, but I recently picked up this Perseverance medallion from the brand, inspired by a vintage signet ring. It scratches the McQueen itch with flying colors.

Secondhand gold is also an option. Alloy Market recently came onto my radar, and I’m browsing it daily for myself and gifts for my wife. They’ve got a small but mighty collection of certified men’s items with pendants and medallions you can mix and match. All of the quality without any of the markup.

Don’t limit yourself to just a medallion, though. Get a little funky. Redford did for a while with this turquoise number that somehow looked even cooler hitting under the sternum. Shinola’s got an option there too. Bali-based Salty Dagger has an Odysseus-approved Greek mythology piece. And why not try a locket, like this one from Pattaraphan. Miansai has a great pendant. Get fancy with the Prevaut diamond ring deal. When in doubt, steal from the girls. I got this With Clarity birthstone necklace for my wife that I might take a swing at myself.

Peyote Bird High Desert Sterling Silver Necklace

Shinola 21mm Turquoise Inlay Tag Necklace

From the abbreviated/slightly bastardized Shakespeare: “All the world’s a stage and one man in his time plays many parts.” Jewelry can feel like a risk, even if you’re following some sort of contrived guide to styling and buying it. Sometimes we pretend until we’re comfortable actually being. Redford and McQueen and company were actors. Pretending was their legacy, and they were good at it. Take a leaf from their book and get dressed for the curtain call.
