#6777. What You Need to Know About Volufiline, Everyone’s Latest Skin Care Obsession

Social media is full of products that promise to transform your face. The latest one making the rounds? Volufiline, an ingredient being likened to natural filler. Guys are swiping and dabbing it onto their undereyes, smile lines, and lips in the hopes of restoring volume and looking younger with no needles, lasers, or scalpels in sight. Fans credit the topical for improvements in undereye hollows and skin quality and making them get carded again. One X user even claims that it looks like “you’ve genuinely gotten a facelift” after two weeks of use.

The pitch is that Volufiline is basically filler in a bottle. But does it actually check out?

Volufiline is a trademarked cosmetic ingredient made with Anemarrhena asphodeloides root extract (a source of the compound sarsasapogenin) and hydrogenated polyisobutene (an emollient that softens and smooths skin). “The theory is that sarsasapogenin encourages fat cells to develop and store more lipids, making them fuller,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, director of cosmetic dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care. Essentially, the hope is to counteract volume loss that naturally occurs as we grow older.

We’ve spent the last year sampling the latest releases in men’s skin care, hair care, and more. Our favorites will help you level up.

In a small study by Sederma, the French company that manufactures Volufiline, 28 women applied a cream containing Volufiline to one breast for 56 days. While the treated breast’s average volume increased by 2.2%, the result wasn’t statistically significant. Kobets also points out that the comparison was with an untreated breast—rather than the same cream without Volufiline—so it’s unclear if Volufiline or other ingredients in the cream drove the increase in volume. Plus, we can’t exactly extrapolate the results seen in a female breast to a man’s face.

Despite the lack of robust clinical evidence supporting its anti-aging claims, Volufiline is the latest topical du jour that people are crediting with their plumper, more supple skin—namely in areas prone to volume loss like the undereyes, smile lines, cheeks, and lips. Some before-and-afters on social media are visually compelling. But the bigger question is whether Volufiline meaningfully increases facial volume or if the improvements are simply due to a temporary plumping effect—or even the other ingredients paired alongside it.

“Some improvement likely comes from the moisturizing formula: hydration softens fine lines, emollients smooth the surface, and that finish changes how light reflects off skin,” Kobets says. (Changes in lighting and specific camera angles can also make the after photos look more striking.) While Volufiline might help your skin look better, the jury’s still out on whether it meaningfully restores lost volume. “Making skin look hydrated and plump isn’t the same as rebuilding the fat underneath it,” Kobets says.

As for those filler in a bottle claims? Alexandra Bowles, DO, a board-certified dermatologist at MONA Dermatology, sets the record straight. “Volufiline is designed to support volume in the skin, and some people may notice slightly plumper, fuller-looking skin over time,” she says. Meanwhile, injectable filler adds immediate volume and structure and can reshape areas like the tear trough, lips, and jawline. “A cream or serum works at the surface and builds gradually, so it can’t create that kind of change,” she says. Read: While it may complement your skin care routine, it won’t replace or replicate results from filler.

Both derms are open to patients experimenting with Volufiline, but with a few caveats. “I think Volufiline is worth trying if you have realistic expectations, but it’s definitely overhyped as an alternative to filler,” Bowles says. If you really want to (pardon the pun) move the needle on undereye hollows, loss of lip volume, or a less-defined jawline, she says carefully placed filler or other in-office treatments may be more effective.

Kobets doesn’t rule out trying Volufiline, either, so long as you’re not expecting to restore facial fat. That said, she advises being cautious if you have a chronic skin condition like eczema or rosacea, or if you’re acne-prone. Try a patch test first and stop if your skin stings or burns.

Bowles suggests prioritizing reputable brands with clear ingredient lists and modest claims around a gradual improvement in the look and feel of skin. Be wary of products that promise instant results, have vague ingredient lists, or come from unverified sellers. “Don’t experiment with raw ingredients or assume a higher percentage works better,” Kobets adds.

The TL;DR: Volufiline is intriguing, but the hype is outpacing the evidence. More rigorous research is needed to address its volume-enhancing claims for facial skin, so take them with a grain of salt. Consistently using a well-formulated product might help your skin look more supple and hydrated; just don’t expect any miracles or a true dupe for injectables. “Good skin care improves skin quality, but it can’t do every job we’re asking of it,” Kobets says.

#6776. The Best Korean Exfoliator to Get (and Maintain) Glass Skin

If there’s one common denominator among Korean skin-care products, be they cleansers or toners, it’s that they prioritize the skin barrier. With this context, the best Korean exfoliators may seem a little counterintuitive—after all, face exfoliants can sometimes do more harm than good, relying on strong active ingredients (or high concentrations) and inadvertently leaving skin dry or irritated.

But that’s the beauty of the Korean approach to resurfacing skin. “K-beauty favors gentle, more frequent exfoliation that protects the skin barrier,” says Jane Yoo, MD, a board-certified dermatologist in New York, NY. “To this effect, K-beauty utilizes low-concentration acids, enzyme powders, or peeling gels that roll dead skin off the surface.” These light-handed exfoliating formulas also considered a critical part of a daily routine aimed towards getting (and maintaining) glass skin—and a natural counterpart to moisturizing. “Exfoliating is usually followed by layers of hydration to support the barrier as the goal is the same: achieve smooth skin but with less irritation,” says Dr. Yoo. With that in mind, consider these worth adding to your regimen.

Exfoliation works on multiple levels to refine and resurface skin—making it one of the most impactful steps in any skin-care routine. At its most basic, “exfoliation helps to remove the outermost layer of dead skin cells in the stratum corneum, promoting skin cell turnover and revealing brighter, smoother and more even-toned skin,” says Dr. Chang.

It can also clear debris from pores, which helps reduce whiteheads, blackheads, and other forms of acne. And in helping shed those dead skin cells that would otherwise pile up on skin’s surface, “exfoliation can also help improve the absorption of active ingredients like vitamin C or retinoids,” she says.

Unlike Western exfoliation habits—which tend to be more aggressive—“Korean skin-care routines emphasize the regular use of gentler topicals to achieve radiant skin without irritation,” says Dr. Chang. One big point of difference is that in the U.S., many formulations tend to focus on correcting issues, be they acne, dullness, or dark spots.

However, Koreans prioritize prevention and consistency. As a result, “you’ll rarely find harsh scrubs or aggressive peels,” says Cho. “The majority of K-beauty exfoliants use mild chemical exfoliants such as PHA, because they clear dead skin cells without irritation.” Fermented enzymes and natural fruit extracts are also popular, since they tend to be well tolerated even by those with sensitive skin, according to Dr. Chang.

How often you exfoliate ultimately depends on your skin type and the sort of exfoliant you’re using. For example, if you have dry or sensitive skin, exfoliating once or twice a week with a mild acid may suffice, says Dr. Chang. Meanwhile, “for those with oily or acne-prone skin, people may tolerate light daily exfoliation with ingredients like salicylic acid,” she says.

Ultimately, the strength of your exfoliant plays a large role. “Higher strength exfoliants should be used less frequently, while very gentle exfoliators could be used daily in those who tolerate it well,” says Dr. Chang. If you’re using a Korean exfoliant, then it’s likely gentle enough to use daily or every other day (but again, that depends). Ultimately, she says, “the key is to monitor for signs of over-exfoliation—like stinging, redness, flaking, or tightness—and adjust the frequency accordingly.”

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to the best Korean exfoliator, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, exfoliant type, and the skin-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend to you.

#6775. Everything You Need to Know About Fiber and Crohn's Disease, According to Dietitians

Just thinking about fiber can make many people with Crohn’s feel nervous. After all certain fiber-rich foods can be tough to tolerate, but the ones that cause trouble aren’t always obvious. Even a seemingly harmless omelet or a fruit smoothie can trigger symptoms in some people. So if you’ve been avoiding the nutrient, that’s understandable—and not uncommon. Research suggests people with Crohn’s tend to eat relatively little fiber, even during remission. One 2015 study found the average daily intake for individuals with the condition was just 16 grams. For context, experts recommend that men aim for 38 grams a day.

But here’s the thing: Having an inflammatory bowel disease doesn’t necessarily mean you should stick to a low-fiber diet. Some studies have found that eating foods rich in the nutrient may actually lower your risk of future flares, improve gut health, and reduce inflammation not only in your gastrointestinal tract but throughout your body.

We get it, though—navigating the sometimes confusing and land-mine-filled world of fiber can feel overwhelming, especially post-flare, and the stakes are high. No one wants to feel crummy or worry about being stuck near a toilet all day. That’s why we asked a group of registered dietitians to answer some of the most pressing questions about Crohn’s and fiber. Here’s what they said about getting enough without upsetting your stomach, which types may be harder to tolerate, and more.

Let’s take a step back and review some nutrition science 101.

In the simplest terms, fiber is a plant-based carbohydrate our bodies cannot fully breakdown or absorb. It resists digestion in the stomach and small intestine and depending on the type, is either partially or fully fermented by gut bacteria in the colon. This makes it different from other nutrients like fats and proteins, which the body breaks down and absorbs.

There are two main types of fiber, each with its own functions and benefits. Here’s a quick overview of each:

What it is: A type of fiber that passes through the GI tract largely intact, adds bulk to stools, helps keep you regular, and aids in regulating blood sugar. Foods rich in insoluble fiber are typically the ones we think of as hard to digest.

Where to find it: Pear and apple skins, raspberries, wheat bran, leafy greens like kale and collard greens, nuts, seeds, and legumes, among other foods.

What it is: A type of fiber that dissolves in water and forms a gel in the gut, slowing carbohydrate absorption. It helps control cholesterol, increases satiety, and makes stools easier to pass.

Where to find it: Beans, oats, barley, carrots, and the flesh of pears, among other foods.

The short answer: yes. But proceed with caution. During an active flare your fiber intake should depend on what you can tolerate, with amounts gradually increasing as symptoms improve.

“The goal is not to eat as much fiber as possible,” says Anya Argosh, MS, RD, a registered dietitian and the founder of Birchwell Clinic. “It’s to build as much dietary variety as your gut can comfortably and safely handle.”

A lower-fiber diet is often recommended during flares to give the GI tract a “rest.” However, Dahlia Marin, RDN, LD, CGN, a registered dietitian specializing in GI issues and co-founder of Married to Health, says limited evidence supports this approach for people without strictures (abnormal narrowings in the GI tract). “Historically, people with active Crohn’s were often told to follow a low-fiber diet, particularly when experiencing diarrhea, abdominal pain, or increased bowel movements. However, current research does not strongly support eliminating all fiber during a flare,” Marin says.

Instead, Marin recommends tailoring food choices to your symptoms and tolerance.

For example, if certain textures are hard for your body to handle, changing how you prepare foods may help.

Consider “choosing well-cooked, peeled, blended, or puréed fruits and vegetables rather than large amounts of raw, fibrous foods,” she says. That might mean roasting carrots or pears instead of eating them raw in a salad or opting for puréed vegetable soup or smoothie.

During a flare foods high in insoluble fiber—such as fruit and vegetable skins, fibrous leafy greens, nuts, seeds, popcorn, and corn on the cob—may also need to be temporarily limited until symptoms improve.

If you have a stricture, eating softer foods or modifying textures, limiting sources of insoluble fiber, and chewing thoroughly are especially important to help reduce the risk of an obstruction. However, fiber tolerance varies from person-to-person and if you have a stricture, you should work with your healthcare provider to come up with an individualized plan.

Kelly L. Burgess, MBA, RD, LDN, the founder of To Better Health LLC and the creator of the HealthyBites HealthyLife app, says she sometimes suggests a low-FODMAP diet during an active flare. This short-term approach may help people whose symptoms are triggered by FODMAPs, fermentable carbohydrates that can be hard on the gut. High-FODMAP foods include certain beans and legumes, as well as vegetables such as cabbage, cauliflower, garlic, and onions, which can cause symptoms like gas and bloating in some people.

A low-FODMAP diet is typically used on a temporary basis in people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) to identify symptom triggers and may help relieve symptoms in people with Crohn’s who have IBS-like symptoms.

Whether you’re coming off a flare or in remission, it’s best to take a “low and slow” approach to adding more fiber to your diet, Argosh says. Introducing too much too quickly can worsen symptoms, leaving you bloated and uncomfortable. “Pace your fiber—don’t force it,” Burgess says. “Begin with small amounts and increase them gradually as tolerated.” In practice, this might mean starting with small portions of well-tolerated fiber-rich foods spread throughout the day, then gradually expanding the types and amounts of fiber you eat at meals and snacks.

Some experts suggest a multi-step approach, starting with easy-to-tolerate, soft fruits, veggies, and grains—think potatoes, white rice, and bananas—and gradually progressing to harder-to-digest salad, seeds, corn, celery and dried fruit.

It’s worth noting that hydration should also increase as fiber intake rises to soften stools and prevent constipation.

When it comes to getting fiber, the dietitians agree that food is generally the best place to start. Fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and other plant foods offer more than just fiber—they also provide other vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants that support overall health and may help with inflammation.

That said fiber supplements can sometimes come in handy, especially when you’re traveling or don’t have access to the foods you typically eat. Finding one that works for you may take some patience, though.

Marin says different supplements can affect your gut in very different ways. “For example, psyllium is a soluble, gel-forming fiber that holds water but is not heavily fermented, while fibers such as inulin and fructooligosaccharides are much more fermentable and can have a greater effect on the gut microbiome.” In practical terms these variations mean one supplement might sit just fine with you and another could leave you feeling gassy or bloated. Which brings us to…

If you’re having trouble eating enough, losing weight without trying, finding yourself cutting out more and more foods, or feeling unsure how to add fiber into your diet after a flare, consider seeing a registered dietitian who specializes in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). These professionals can help you get the nutrients you need while figuring out which foods and textures work best for you so you don’t unnecessarily restrict your diet. They can also check for nutrient deficiencies and help tailor your diet if you have a stricture, have had surgery for Crohn’s, or are dealing with other Crohn's complications.

A registered dietitian can also help you identify your trigger foods. Triggers generally vary from person to person, which can make them tricky to pin down. Some people tolerate oats and nuts, while others can’t eat either. The same goes for raw fruit and veggies, whole grains, and other fiber-containing foods. It comes down to trial and error: figuring out what works for you—and what doesn’t.

Your gastroenterologist should be involved if you have new or worsening symptoms, particularly if you’re experiencing persistent abdominal pain, frequent diarrhea, blood in your stool, unexplained weight loss, worsening fatigue, and/or vomiting. Get urgent medical attention if you have severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, abdominal swelling, or can’t pass stool or gas. These can be signs of an intestinal obstruction, which is especially important to watch for in people with Crohn’s-related strictures.

#6773. Pierpaolo Piccioli Is Stepping Down From Balenciaga

After just 16 months, the creative director and the brand are parting ways

After less than two years, Pierpaolo Piccioli is stepping down from Balenciaga, where he had been tasked with interpreting the house’s legacy of sculptural elegance without alienating the streetwear superfans his predecessor, Demna, courted.

Piccioli entered Balenciaga amidst the creative director roundabout of last year, a moment when many major fashion brands shuffled leadership. His debut, shown in the spring 2026 season, explored Balenciaga’s signature sack silhouette with simple evening dresses and separates alongside sculpted leather outerwear and bubble-hemmed skirts—all styled with space-age sunglasses and long leather gloves.

Throughout subsequent collections, he continued to chase an idea of pragmatic beauty. For Spring 2027, he showed elevated, voluminous versions of familiar ensembles like a T-shirt and jeans. Through that tenure, he courted high-profile fans like Meghan Markle and Tessa Thompson.

Born in 1967 in Italy, Piccioli studied fashion at the Istituto Europeo di Design in Rome. He interned at Brunello Cuccinelli before joining the team at Fendi, working alongside his design school friend Maria Grazia Chiuri, who would become his long-term creative partner. After roughly a decade, the pair went to Valentino to lead the accessories department in 1999; they were appointed co-creative directors of the brand in 2008. In 2016, Chiuri left to helm Dior, leaving Piccioli to lead the brand on his own.

There, he really established his legacy as a beacon of elegance and a maestro with color. Each season, he offered a new palette that encouraged audiences to rethink the rainbow—and how to pair its individual shades. His fall 2022 collection was rendered almost entirely in shocking pink, earning him a Pantone shade dubbed “Pink PP.” His couture collections in particular were celebrations of fashion, often eliciting tears from the audience—most notably from vocal fan Celine Dion. Yes, they were fantastical, but just wearable enough to keep shoppers returning to stores. After roughly 25 years at Valentino, he departed in 2024—then went to Balenciaga in 2025.

Cristóbal Balenciaga founded his namesake label in 1917 in San Sebastian, Spain, reestablishing his couture house in Paris in 1937. Often referred to as an “architect” of fashion rather than a designer, he is remembered for a vision rooted in shape above all. He cast the corsetry of the time aside and dealt instead in the manipulation of volume and silhouette. His creations were both sculptural and fluid, with iconic shapes including the “tunic” and “sack” silhouettes. His legacy was carried on by subsequent directors Michel Goma, Alexander Wang, and most notably, Nicolas Ghesquière and then Demna.

In theory, it could have been a great match for Piccioli. But Demna, who helmed Balenciaga from 2015 to 2025, turned those founding principles upside down. Unlike Cristóbal, he designed with satire top of mind. The designer injected his singular vision from his very early days on the job, creating collections that blended the classic codes of Cristóbal with his own signature high-low, European club-kid aesthetic. In doing so, he transformed the French fashion house into a mega-brand beloved by a spectrum of superfans across both menswear and womenswear. And that is a difficult consumer base to turn away from.

Piccioli had what was undeniably a difficult job, one rather symptomatic of the current state of fashion in which creative-director shakeups have become so commonplace. Three seasons is a very short time to establish a new look for a fashion brand, especially a sales behemoth like Balenciaga. Piccioli is immensely talented, and we look forward to whatever he has in store for us next.

#6772. Met Gala 2027: Costume Institute Announces New Theme After John Galliano Controversy

The 2027 Met Gala has a new focus. On November 5, Vogue, alongside the Metropolitan Museum of Art Costume Institute, announced its new spring 2027 exhibition and Met Gala theme. And its new focus is on the “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” which will be curated by Andrew Bolton alongside Stephanie Kramer and Emily Mushaben. This pivot comes after designer John Galliano pulled out of the 2027 Met Gala months after political and civic leaders raised concerns over his previous racist and antisemitic comments that led to his termination as Dior’s creative director in 2011.

The exhibition will be “devoted to the undersung beauty and allure of quotidian garments—think the aforementioned t-shirts and jeans, plus raincoats, sweatshirts, puffer jackets, and more. It will ask visitors ‘to see the everyday anew, and come at its subject from two perspectives: First, exploring how designers have reinvented and elevated archetypal garments to runway-worthy creations and then, secondly, highlight how humble, even ‘disposable’ materials—like paper, aluminum, and plastic—are transformed into wearable art.”

“It was really important to come up with an exhibition that wasn’t just a masterwork show or something that we could do a little bit more easily,” Bolton also said. “That was really important to me: to come up with an idea that wasn’t a substitute. And it had to have some sort of contemporary resonance.”

Before this switch, the museum stated that the original exhibit, John Galliano: Horizons, was meant to “consider how artistic achievement should be understood alongside ethical accountability.” So now, this exploration of the extraORDINARY seems to be more focused on design and creation from a more sustainable viewpoint.

So now that fashion’s biggest night is back on track with a new theme in hand, it will be interesting to see how all our favorite celebrities interpret this new theme. The Met Gala 2027 will take place on May 3, and the exhibit will open to the public on May 9, 2027, and run through January 9, 2028.

Aiyana Ishmael is the style editor at Cosmopolitan magazine. In her work, Aiyana focuses on the culture of fashion and how it intertwines and shapes the zeitgeist. She is an award-winning journalist from Miami, Florida, and a graduate of the historically Black university, Florida A&M. She is a 2024 Forbes 30 Under 30: Media honoree, and her debut romance novella PASSING GAME is set to release March of 2027 (831 Stories/Simon & Schuster).

#6771. Coty Sales Decline 2% as Transition Kicks In

For Coty’s first quarter 2027 earnings, the 2% like-for-like sales decline shows an improvement on the last year, when revenues fell 6% and 4% in the first and second halves of fiscal 2026, respectively. The stabilization — sales were at -1% in Q4 2026 — can be credited to growth in key markets like the US, Asia-Pacific and Latin America, as well as fruitful reinvestment in the group’s prestige business that includes Burberry, Hugo Boss and Calvin Klein.

Still, executive chair and interim CEO Markus Strobel was careful to refer to the progress as “green shoots”, which he hopes will translate into positive growth over time. “As we’ve previously shared, 2027 will be a transition year,” he said in a statement released on Wednesday. “We expect the recovery to be uneven, and implementation will take time. We know confidence is earned through consistent delivery, and our goal is to steadily improve execution and translate it into shareholder value in the years ahead.”

Coty.Curated, the French beauty group’s turnaround framework, kicked into motion last fiscal year. A redesign of the organization and cost structure hopes to improve conversion through reinvestment into its portfolio of brands.

The strategy is paying off the most in the prestige segment. Net revenues declined 1% to $1.1 billion in Q1, a contrast to the same quarter a year prior (-4%), and representing 68% of total sales. “We have increasingly concentrated investment behind our top six prestige brands — Burberry, Hugo Boss, Calvin Klein, Marc Jacobs, Chloé, and Kylie Cosmetics — which represented 73% of prestige sales in Q1,” Strobel noted, highlighting the success of new launches including Boss Bottled Beyond for Her, Burberry Goddess Amber Vanilla, Mood Stones by Kylie Jenner, and makeup from Marc Jacobs Beauty.

Earlier this week, Coty announced a 40-year extension of its Marc Jacobs license, which it has held since 2003. The plan is to expand the brand across multiple categories following the successful relaunch of Marc Jacobs Beauty in May. (The beauty offshoot was discontinued in 2021, once its licensing deal with LVMH-owned Kendo ended.)

Strobel said: “The recent launch of Marc Jacobs Beauty makeup is off to a strong start across the US, the UK, Canada, and Australia. The agreement provides Coty with a strong platform to build on that momentum while enhancing the long-term visibility of Coty’s Prestige portfolio.”

The recovery of consumer beauty — including CoverGirl, Rimmel, and Sally Hansen — is slightly slower. While the decline in like-for-like sales narrowed to 3% from 8% in the first half of fiscal 2026, the segment remains negative. Net revenues reached $496.8 million in Q1, declining 3% on a like-for-like basis.

Asia-Pacific led growth across both segments, with sales up 8% to $192 million, driven by higher sales in China, Southeast Asia, and Asia travel retail. Sales were flat across the Americas at $653 million, with particular momentum in Brazil. EMEA (Europe, the Middle East, and Africa) revenues fell 5% to $710 million; the group cited lower sales in the Middle East and Europe.

Coty expects to see a low single-digit decline in Q2, consistent with the last two quarters. As for the full year, the company is still withholding its projection as it gears up to claw back the negative growth seen throughout 2026.

#6769. One of My Least Favorite Politicians Lost an Election This Week. I Can’t Stop Laughing About It.

This guy was an ur-Trumper before Trump, and I’m so glad we’re rid of him.

This one is for me. Pardon me while I bust a gut.

Kris Kobach of Kansas—and never has a phrase with three K’s been more apt—is one of the founding weasels of the modern voter-suppression effort. If there is an odious policy position concocted since 2008, Kobach has run the laboratory that produced it. Imaginary voter fraud? Kobach led the farcical election-integrity commission during Trump I that fell apart after a contentious 2017 hearing in New Hampshire at which Kobach’s contentions were disemboweled by Maine secretary of state Matthew Dunlap. Draconian immigration policies? As Kansas secretary of state, Kobach tried to initiate a “proof of citizenship” law that lined him up on the wrong side of the League of Women Voters. Outright racism? Kobach told a radio program that the Obama administration was not far from a call for an end to all prosecutions of African Americans. If there was an ur-Trumper before Trump, it was Kris Kobach.

I thought we were rid of him when he ran for governor in 2018 and lost. I thought we were rid of him when he ran for the Senate in 2020 and lost. I thought we were rid of him when he got tangled up with Steve Bannon’s Build the Wall scam. But he was like the shingles virus in the body politic. He got elected Kansas attorney general in 2022.

And, on Tuesday, and extending into Thursday afternoon, it looks as though Kris Kobach might have lost another election. May it be his last.

#6767. The Met Gala 2027 Theme “extraORDINARY,” Explained

Love jeans and t-shirts? This one’s for you.

Today, the Metropolitan Museum of Art announced that its spring 2027 Costume Institute exhibition and Met Gala will be devoted to familiar garments and commonplace materials rendered remarkable via the interventions of designers. Organized by Curator in Charge Andrew Bolton, with assistance from Stephanie Kramer and Emily Mushaben, the Met Gala 2027 theme, “extraORDINARY: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday,” will ask its visitors “to see the everyday anew.” It will come at its subject from two directions, one focusing on the elevation of archetypal garments, i.e. the above-mentioned tees and jeans, and the the other examining how humble, even “disposable” materials, from paper to aluminum to plastic, are transformed into wearable art.

The exhibition replaces the John Galliano blockbuster originally planned for 2027 that was subsequently canceled after it became a cultural flashpoint.

“I didn’t have a plan B,” Bolton says candidly. “It was really important to come up with an exhibition that wasn’t just a masterwork show or something that we could do a little bit more easily. I wanted it to be as challenging and as provocative and as beautiful as a John show would have been.” He continues: “That was really important to me: to come up with an idea that wasn’t a substitute. And it had to have some sort of contemporary resonance.”

Bolton went back to “Costume Art,” the Costume Institute’s 2026 show as a starting point. That exhibition “placed the dressed body at the center of aesthetic experience,” he says, “and I suppose it led me to think more about how we experience clothing in everyday life through habit and touch and movement and sensation.”

Pieces from Jun Takahashi’s fall 2024 Undercover show will greet guests at the entrance to “extraORDINARY.”

The final gallery will feature the work of Anrealage’s Kuniko Moringa.

Both of these pieces are from the fall 2024 Anrealage collection.

In that sense, “extraORDINARY” dovetails with a movement across the recent fashion shows in which designers embraced real, recognizable clothes and platformed individuality—soul, you could even call it—via their styling. “Quiet gestures hold so much more meaning than the louder gestures,” Bolton says. “Bravado—we should be looking at the opposite of that.”

He was drawn in particular to the Japanese designer Jun Takahashi’s fall 2024 Undercover collection, a sublimely moving show that was inspired by Wim Wenders’s contemplative film about the beauty of everyday life, Perfect Days, and included a spoken poem specially written for the occasion by the director about the daily rituals of a single mother, “Watching a Working Woman.” Garments from Takahashi’s collection—otherwise unremarkable pieces reworked via collage and layering techniques that rendered them anything but prosaic—will greet visitors at the entrance to “extraORDINARY.” They “give the exhibition a real human starting point,” Bolton says.

The show will close with the work of another Japanese designer, Anrealage’s Kunihiko Morinaga, whose “unfamiliar geometries” and “unexpected proportions” add a conceptual dimension to what is otherwise familiar. Rain parkas and trench coats as “objects of wonder.”

Jonathan Anderson’s Loewe, spring 2022 ready-to-wear

Moncler 1 by Pierpaolo Piccioli, fall 2019

Helmut Lang, spring 1993. (Photo by Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Penske Media via Getty Images)

In between, “Familiar Forms” will look more closely at designers’ interventions of common items—Virgil Abloh’s Off-White t-shirts, Gianfranco Ferré’s demonstrative white shirts, trenches from Jonathan Anderson at Loewe and “the different designers at Burberry,” and puffer gowns from Pierpaolo Piccioli’s collections for Moncler all of which, one way of the other, “put the extra in the ordinary,” Bolton says.

“Common Matter,” meanwhile, will delve into the potential of throwaway materials and found objects as actual garments. Margiela will be prominent in this gallery, alongside other designers who have made a habit of repurposing materials. “A paper dress,” Bolton says, can demand as much skill and as much labor as a silk gown. And the cost of a material tells us very little about the craftsmanship required to transform it. Reuse and reconstruction run through the exhibition because I’m interested in how things acquire life and how that changes what we value and care for.”

A dress made from paper. Comme des Garçons, spring 1992 ready-to-wear

A silverware bodice. Maison Margiela, spring 2027 ready-to-wear

Questions of value, consumption, and resourcefulness give the exhibition a particular urgency, Bolton feels. “It will make us question: what do we overlook, what do we discard, what makes something worth keeping?” I think that fashion is so often associated with the pursuit of the new and the ephemeral that I’m really interested in how possibilities can emerge through returning to familiar things. I think there’s something hopeful about discovering how much imagination the everyday can hold.”

If that doesn’t have the promise of Galliano’s fantastic and radical reimaginings, it is not merely the humdrum we’ll be talking about. Among the pieces bound to amuse and delight are a splintered china ensemble from Martin Margiela and Ellen Hodakova Larsson’s next-generation jangly spoon dress.

Jeans and a cotton tank that aren’t really jeans and a cotton tank, but leather. From Matthieu Blazy’s Bottega Veneta debut for fall 2022.

The exhibition, which opens to the public on May 9, 2027 after the Met Gala on May 3 and will be on view through January 9, 2028, is being conceptualized by the London-based scenographic design studio, 1009, with the intention of creating a dialogue between the installation and the people that will move among it. “I want the visitors to be part of the exhibition,” Bolton says. In fact, if he had his way, the show itself, not just the red carpet ball that precedes it, would have a dress code. He likes the idea of people wearing “their favorite t-shirt or their favorite pair of jeans or their favorite hoodie” as they navigate their way through the show. “There’ll be a humanity to it,” he says.

“extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday” will be sponsored by Instagram, with major funding from Moncler, and additional support from Condé Nast. Education programs presented in conjunction with the exhibition are made possible by Jordan Roth.

A Junya Watanabe fall 2011 biker will be showcased in the “Familiar Forms” room.

#6766. Silver Fox at 16. How Men Are Embracing Gray Hair at Every Age

At 16, James Chudley’s first gray hair was spotted by the girl sitting next to him in Biology. He thought it was a joke. She took a photo to prove it. There it was: one silver thread, just above his ear. “For the rest of the year,” he says, “every Biology lesson, it was: ‘Oh, there’s another one!’”

Chudley, now a personal trainer-in-training from Surrey, England wasn’t too bothered. “I thought I’d just pluck it out,” he says. By 19, though, there were too many to pluck. An anti-gray shampoo turned his bath blue; dye was another option, but he had reservations: “I didn’t want to end up looking like Dracula.”

Away from school, Chudley gradually got comfortable with his grays. Even so, he mentioned them before anyone else could, “almost as a defense mechanism.” Usually the response was playful roasting, sometimes even a compliment. But then someone would catch him off guard. Chudley, now 22, was recently working as a delivery driver when a customer looked him up and down. “Bit young to be going gray, isn’t it?” she said. Almost as an afterthought, she added, “Is it stressing you out?”

Gray hair is an inevitability for most men. Live long enough, and the color starts to drain. For many people, that begins in their early 30s and becomes more visible with age. By 50, suggests a study by the British Association of Dermatologists, up to 23% of us will have half a head of gray hair. The science is straightforward. Hair follicles contain melanocytes, the cells responsible for producing pigment. As we age, the stem cells that replenish them become less active, and the color fades. It’s like a printer cartridge running out of ink: the paper keeps coming, but eventually, there’s nothing on there.

Going gray in your teens and early 20s, however, is another matter. It’s relatively uncommon, although anecdotes are easy to find. Spend five minutes on TikTok and you’ll see plenty asking why they’re suddenly gray. Reddit has versions too, with users swapping stories and theories about why they—and seemingly everyone around them—are losing their color so young. “I don’t know if you’ve noticed, but people’s hair seems to be turning white really fast lately,” says one post. “How did we end up in the worst century where literally anything can go wrong?”

It’s hard to say if we’re actually going gray earlier, or if it’s just that more people are talking about it. The theories, meanwhile, keep on coming—from mineral deficiencies to heavy-metal exposure. There’s also an optimistic explanation: More people are open to embracing it.

Young men are spending more money than ever on looking good—even on their grays. Rather than shopping for cheap cover-ups, they are forensically researching science-backed cosmetics. Part of this also means a rejection of chemical-heavy products and a more skeptical attitude towards unnecessary cosmetics. Hair dye, after all, is not entirely harmless.

Online communities like “Gray and Proud” and “Silver Revolution” have tens of thousands of members. Paul Mescal and Jeremy Allen White have also done their part for gray-hair representation among young(ish) people: The Times dubbed them “silver fox cubs.”

Maybe things really are shifting. But if the demand for anti-gray products is any indication, the revolution is still a way off. Anti-gray serums are becoming big business. The global market is expected to jump from around $1.3 billion to $2 billion by 2031, according to Deep Market Insights. Cosmetics Business magazine calls it the “next men’s grooming trend,” with growing interest in peptide-based products. On the internet, you see both sides. On Reddit, a 26-year-old guy shares a photo of his gray head of hair, saying that he’s already got more than his dad. The top comment reads: “Do your due diligence, of course—bloodwork, diet etc.” Someone else follows up with: “[Guys] with gray hair are [hot].”

One person making the case for Gen Z’s grey-haired men is model and musician Charlie Jeer. The 24-year-old first found fame on the Netflix dating show Too Hot to Handle. He has the chiseled jawline and cheekbones of a conventional heartthrob, but there’s another feature viewers can’t seem to get past: his hair. “I feel like it gets brought up in conversation every single day in my life,” he says.

Jeer first noticed the grays as a teenager, and mostly shrugged off the comments. Online, it’s a different story. “Why are you going gray?”; “Can’t tell if bro is 15 or 60; ” “Err this old man.” “It’s relentless,” he says.

Now, Jeer sees the grays as an opportunity to stand out. They’ve helped build his profile as a model, too, partly because of the “age ambiguity” they give him. He’s picked up credits with brands like Davidoff and Adidas. “There’s a massive commercial potential for me to make a black hair dye and just start marketing that,” he says. “I never did because I was like, ‘No, I’m proud of my hair the way it is.’”

On TikTok, Jeer takes on his critics with captions like: “Joke’s on them when I’m a silver fox by 30.” He really likes it when he hears from other young guys going gray. “I’ve had a little gray-haired community of people come forward and present themselves,” he says. “It’s nice to hear someone else say that they’ve had people come at them for being gray-haired and that they’re going to continue to wear it with confidence.”

Jeer might be on the young end of the gray-hair population, but as a guy, he’s riding a well-worn track. Men have always been afforded the privilege of associating their grays with looking more distinguished. You don’t have to be George Clooney (or a Too Hot to Handle contestant) to benefit from that. Women, meanwhile, aren’t part of that deal: gray hair is more often simply read as old, an obviously unfair double standard.

It still come with baggage for men, though: age, lost virility, fading relevance. “The first gray” is practically a trope in its own right—a visual shorthand in films, books and TV for a character beginning to age, often followed by the inevitable midlife crisis. There are dozens of those scenes, in everything from The Simpsons to Vanilla Sky.

Matt Newman is a New York–based hairstylist who hates his gray hair. “There are so many examples of men with premature grays that people love and adore,” he says. “But in your 20s, that might not be an aesthetic you’re ready to dive into.”

Perhaps that’s why Jackass star Johnny Knoxville waited until 49 to finally embrace his natural hair color. He started going gray in his 20s and dyed it for most of his life. Then, during lockdown, he asked his wife to give him a buzz cut to reveal the silver underneath, on Instagram. “I should start a challenge but I don’t want to call anyone out,” he wrote on Instagram. Going gray, declared one Mr. Porter headline, was now a “punk power move”.

That’s not quite how Saavan Varambhia, 25, a data analyst from Buckinghamshire, would have described it. Not at first, anyway. Like Chudley, he was at school when a group of female friends spotted his grays and tried to pluck them out. “I was like, ‘Hmm, I don’t know how I feel about this,’” he says. A few years later, he had enough gray hairs on his head to “stop people in their tracks.”

For Varambhia, the contrast was hard to miss. He’s South Asian, with naturally deep-black hair, so the grays stood out. The Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology reports that people of Asian descent also tend to go gray later, often in their late 30s. According to Professor Desmond Tobin, a professor of dermatological science at University College Dublin, many Eastern cultures have traditionally been less accepting of grays than the West, with men and women both more likely to dye them.

“At first, I felt like I didn’t want to seem a lot older than my peers,” Varambhia says. Over time, though, he came to see the silver as something that set him apart. “I’ve always been one to stand out, and it was another attributing factor to that.”

When there are too many gray hairs to pluck, do you reach for the Just for Men, or join the silver fox cub club?

Turning gray at any age can make you wonder why it’s happening. According to Tobin, the answer is usually in your DNA. “The first thing to do is just to look at your [previous] generation of relatives,” he says. “They’re going to give you a road map for where you’re going to be. And if you have early grayers—teens, early 20s—then that’s really mapped out quite starkly in the family.”

Other things can speed up the process, too. Stress is a big one. Tobin says it can damage the cells responsible for producing hair pigment, acting like a “sledgehammer” if the process has already begun. Just look at Barack Obama’s hair before and after his time in the White House. Nutrition can play a role, too, and a blood test can pick up any deficiencies. But Tobin says the nutritional deficiencies linked to premature graying tend to show up in countries where malnutrition is more widespread.

Crucially, though, Tobin says he hasn’t seen hard evidence that young people are going gray earlier across the board. Modern life might come with its share of chronic stressors, he points out, but humans have been enduring trying times since long before social media, climate change, and cost of living crises entered the picture.

Tobin is skeptical of the “overstated claims” made by supplements and serums that promise to “tickle your stem cells.” If you want to slow the process, he says, your best bet is the boring stuff: less stress, plenty of sleep and an antioxidant-rich diet. That might hold things off for a while. But for anyone genetically predisposed to graying, it might not make that much of a difference.

“Would maximum antioxidant intake really stop somebody from graying who’s genetically headed that way? It’s not likely to be a very significant contributor,” Tobin says. “It might, in a multi-prong way, add up to something, but if you’re graying significantly in your teens, that is probably the die that’s being cast for you.”

The good news? Going gray early doesn’t mean the rest of you is aging at the same rate. In fact, there may be a silver lining. People who go gray prematurely are more likely to keep their hair; “nearly all people who bald [do so] with their natural hair color,” says Tobin.

But for anyone who doesn’t want to live with their grays, the hunt for a treatment is on. Research into gray hair has surged alongside the wider boom in longevity science. Tobin says the past five years have felt like a return to the 1980s, when the topical hair-regrowth drug Rogaine first shook up the haircare world. He has consulted for startups developing anti-gray treatments aimed at reducing oxidative stress or extending the life of melanocyte stem cells. The science is promising, but so far, nothing has produced evidence strong enough to satisfy regulators.

Researchers are beginning to understand that graying may not be irreversible, as once thought. Melissa Harris at the University of Alabama has studied the melanocyte stem cells behind hair pigmentation, and immunotherapy as a way to reverse graying. Other research has shown that some hairs can spontaneously regain their pigment, with changes appearing to track periods of stress. It hints that some aspects of aging may be less linear than we assume.

Dr. Greg Williams, a hair restoration surgeon at the Farjo Hair Institute, has watched the field develop. He hosts conference sessions on gray hair and, a couple of years ago, set up a WhatsApp group where specialists around the world could swap ideas and compare notes. “Gray hair is very poorly understood,” he says. “There’s not a lot of research in humans around it.” Maybe that’s surprising, given how universal it seems to be. But commercial fallout is huge. The global hair-and scalp-care industry is worth nearly $9.4 billion, and Williams thinks anyone who figures it out “would be a Nobel Prize winner”.

As for Varambhia, the science seems to fit his experience. Genetics are clearly part of the picture: his dad’s hair has been white for years, and he still has a full head of it. Varambhia also suspects stress sped things up. His grays arrived rapidly as he settled into corporate nine-to-five life. Since hitting the gym regularly, he thinks the process may have slowed.

Knowing other people going through the same thing has helped. “I know eventually I’ll go fully gray. I hope it’s a bit later on than sooner,” he says. But when the time comes? “I’ll embrace it.”

A version of this story originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of British GQ with the title “Gray Ahead of Schedule”

#6765. Kim Kardashian’s Morning Show Look Is a Vintage Paco Rabanne Pastille Party Dress

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Good morning, Kim Kardashian! Starting off a day of press appointments in New York City, the reality star-turned-actor joined her fellow All’s Fair costars on Good Morning America to promote the legal drama’s second season. And while most of us need a cup of coffee (or two) to get ourselves dressed and out the door, she woke up and slipped straight into a vintage Paco Rabanne party dress.

The look, styled by Law Roach, was an intricate peach gown pulled from the Spring/Summer 1989 couture collection. The top was crafted from hundreds of metal discs, which were stitched together to create a one-shoulder silhouette with a side cutout, making for an asymmetrical, backless piece of armor. From the waist, a long silk-crepe skirt floated to the ankle, where it was met by little heeled sandals with clear PVC straps.

The piece of history was sourced by Maison Vintage Virtuoso, a Paris-based archival studio focused on couture, and was reportedly introduced to Kardashian’s team four months ago. (The same ensemble recently sold for nearly $11,500 on 1st Dibs.)

On GMA, Kardashian shared several candid stories from her time filming All’s Fair, and even revealed that she thought Sarah Paulson’s lower-register on-camera voice was her real voice until just a few weeks ago. Despite this confession, the costars were some of the closest on set, and often made one another break character. “They made Sarah and I one time get up and take a walk around the building because they said we needed to get it together,” the Skims founder told the talk show. “We were laughing so hard.”

Kardashian, who later changed into a sheer knit minidress from Dolce and Gabbana’s Autumn/Winter 1997 collection, has curated a press tour wardrobe full of custom gowns (Ashi Studio), vintage pieces (Todd Oldham), and standout couture looks (Schiaparelli).

#6764. Can You Manifest a Husband?

This spring, singer Natalie Imbruglia joined Elizabeth Day on her How to Fail podcast to discuss, among other things, how she manifested her husband. The clip predictably made the rounds online, and it got me thinking about the mechanics of calling in a partner. It’s easy enough to enchant your life with inspirational buzzwords, but sometimes the spell lacks teeth—or worse, you attract someone who matches your checklist on paper but operates on an entirely different wavelength. (You asked for a multilingual finance professional who loves dogs; the universe delivered an auditor who speaks Latin and brought three untamed Dobermans to drinks.)

Pop culture has taken note. On The Kardashians, Kim revealed she learned manifestation techniques from Michael Jackson to draw in aligned suitors, while Khloé echoed the sentiment, treating it as a baseline tool to shape the dynamic she wants. Been there, done that. To cut through the noise, I turned to practicing experts—happily partnered, naturally—for the real rituals and energetic groundwork required to call in a mate.

For many, myself included, previous attempts at manifesting love hit speed bumps: the timing was off, or the wish list wasn't nearly specific enough—ask the universe for someone “adventurous and spontaneous,” and you might end up conjuring an unemployed DJ who doesn’t own a bed frame. In Day’s case, her mother’s friend Lizzie advised her to write down her romantic non-negotiables in ink, then burn the page to release the intention to the universe. It worked—eventually. Magic is an iterative sport, requiring trial, error, and honest self-assessment. Here is what my coven of experts suggests.

The starting point is radical specificity. “Sit down and have a conversation with your heart,” advises astrologer Narayana Montufar, author of Written in Your Stars. She recommends taking pen to paper to define what a true life partner looks like, stripped of outside expectations. “Most of us carry preconceived notions about what marriage is, which may not even be ours,” she explains. Because the universe responds to energetic resonance rather than superficial wish lists, your birth chart can provide a clear roadmap: “Look at your Moon sign for nurturance, your Venus sign for attraction, and your Mars sign for sexual chemistry.”

Equally crucial is auditing past missteps. Astrologer Renee Watt urges taking stock of where prior relationships unraveled and what red flags were brushed aside. “It's possible you've prioritized traits that are ‘sexy’ over qualities that actually contribute to sustainable connections,” she notes, emphasizing that unaddressed jealousy, passivity, or fear will sabotage even the most celestial match. “Once you've gained a strong awareness of what you no longer wish to carry or attract, banish it.”

Once the mental slate is clear, ritual grounds the intention. Corbin Chamberlin, founder of Sage & Salt perfumery, recommends beginning on a Friday—traditionally Venus’s day of love. “Take a cleansing salt bath,” he suggests. “Afterward, write down the qualities you want to receive in a marriage, then the qualities you’re prepared to give in return.” Fold the page toward you three times, place it beneath a white candle, and recite: ‘I make space for a love I can recognize, receive, and return.’ Chamberlin also emphasizes backing magic up with physical space: clear a drawer, a nightstand, or a section of closet to signal you have room for another person in your life.

For astrologer Lauren Ash, intentional jewelry serves as a daily talisman. “Marriage is about much more than jewelry, but a ring is something you see and feel throughout the day,” she says. Different fingers govern different planetary energies: the thumb aligns with Mars for bold initiative; the index finger channels Jupiter for expansion; and the middle finger invokes Saturn for structure and enduring commitment. “The hand matters, too,” Ash adds. “The right hand is what you’re putting out into the world, and the left is what you’re inviting in. You could wear rose quartz on your right ring finger to signal receptivity, and a stone tied to your ideal partner’s Sun or Venus on your left.”

To bolster your environment, Watt recommends burning pink candles for affection, incorporating stones like rhodochrosite and green aventurine, or wearing essential oils of rose and geranium. Montufar also suggests syncing visual meditations with the New Moon, capitalizing on its monthly cycle of clean slates and quiet momentum.

Yet every practitioner shares the same non-negotiable caveat: the real work happens internally before any match arrives. “Before you do the ritual to call in a partner, do the ritual for yourself,” Chamberlin cautions. “We spend so much time thinking about what we want to attract, but very little thinking about our capacity to receive and maintain it. Manifestation isn’t just asking for something—it’s preparing yourself for its arrival.”

That preparation often means shedding rigid aesthetics. “Keep an open mind,” Watt advises, noting that fixating on identical tastes in music or film can blind you to a genuine connection. “My husband holds very little resemblance to any fantasies I once carried in my head, but he's consistent, supportive, and makes me laugh. Before he came into the picture, what I thought I wanted didn't align with what I actually needed.”

At its core, calling in a partner demands unshakeable confidence in the outcome and the emotional stability to hold space for them when they arrive. As Montufar points out, trust is the real engine behind attraction: the clearer your belief that the universe is tuned in, the sharper the results. I’ve previously manifested the exact right match on paper only to watch it collapse because I lacked the grounding to sustain it. Doing the internal homework is where the actual sorcery begins. Happy manifesting, witches.

#6762. Why Do We Keep Coming Back to Godzilla?

Like most people born in the western world after 1954, I knew of a monster named Godzilla before I’d heard of a country called Japan. It’s not a rare perspective. For as long as nearly any living person can remember, Godzilla has been hugely popular, far exceeding the global recognition afforded most leaders, athletes, and certainly his human co-stars, those men and women whose dramatic dealings are the universally agreed-upon bargain for apocalyptic havoc that millions upon millions have gladly paid to see for over 70 years.

What Godzilla hasn’t been is prestigious. The irradiated dinosaur of very few words—mainly deafening screams—is a beloved figure more in the key of Harry Potter, Batman, or James Bond than the loftier fare that typically gets recognized by major festivals or awards bodies. But exceptions to the rule do exist. The Criterion Collection issued Ishiro Honda's 1954 original on a deluxe Blu-ray in 2012 and marked their 1,000th release with a lavish set of Godzilla’s Shōwa era (1954-1975), which both documents film history and calls to mind John Huston’s Chinatown line about sticking around long enough to become respectable. Writing an introduction to Honda’s biography A Life in Film, from Godzilla to Kurosawa, Martin Scorsese deemed the series’ first director "an extraordinary artist and craftsman" and placed Honda’s 1954 film (alongside spin-offs Mothra and Rodan) among “pictures that haunted the imaginations of young moviegoers like myself and millions of others for years to come.” Kiyoshi Kurosawa—perhaps Japan’s greatest living filmmaker, and certainly its finest practitioner of austere horror—deemed Honda’s film an early lesson in national trauma. Thomas Pynchon, too, had ambitious plans to write a novel about the insurance adjuster who responds to Godzilla’s wreckage (the idea never fully materialized, though it did become a nice tangent in his 1990 novel Vineland). We can look at the films and countenance such appreciations from geniuses. In the meantime, good luck to anyone counting the exact number of action figures, coloring books, sticker packs, and lunchboxes boasting Godzilla and friends.

A critical shift started somewhere in the last decade. Toho ostensibly shelved Godzilla with 2004’s Final Wars, a grand finale that was the big-budget equivalent of a child smashing toys. (That is a compliment.) Godzilla LLC boasts enough films and ancillary products to be financially solvent until the sun burns out (or an indomitable monster rises from the sea), but that retirement was short-lived. Toho resurrected the franchise in aggressive form with 2016’s Shin Godzilla, both a complete series reboot and (across several stages, each grotesque and terrifying) character reinvention that dispensed with typical monster-movie hijinks. An unholy experiment that would make the series’ many mad scientists proud, Shin Godzilla fused the hilarious bureaucratic hallway-rushing of In the Loop or Veep with cosmic horror befitting its director, Hideaki Anno, whose contributions to Japanese culture are nearly Godzilla’s equal on the strength of Neon Genesis Evangelion alone. With time, it’s downright eerie to see Anno’s foreshadowing of the global unrest of Trump, Brexit, COVID, and our endless misinformation era. But rather than keep the great filmmaker on retainer for any number of sequels or spin-offs, Toho regrettably followed Shin Godzilla with an anime trilogy produced for Netflix, a rare class of films I’ve been too embarrassed to even log on Letterboxd.

Whether genius or dreck, none of these films quite anticipated 2023’s Godzilla Minus One. It’s one thing to become the highest-grossing Japanese-language release in U.S. history—any Godzilla movie that doesn't at least aim for such a distinction isn’t worth its salt. It’s harder to imagine anyone, even or especially the franchise’s most ardent fans, anticipated lavish public praise from a quintet of Best Director winners in Steven Spielberg (who claims to have seen the film at least three times), James Cameron (who offered to work on a sequel), Christopher Nolan, Guillermo Del Toro, and Bong Joon-ho. In a recorded conversation with Yamazaki, Tom Cruise and Christopher McQuarrie credited the film as an inspiration; the actor went so far as to call it “perfect.” Which is to say nothing of the fact that Godzilla Minus One earned the series its first Oscar, a VFX prize awarded to none other than writer-director Takashi Yamazaki—a nice encapsulation of the film’s balance between spirit and spectacle.

Because Godzilla Minus One resonated more than anyone could have anticipated, Godzilla Minus Zero, which arrives in theaters this weekend, shoulders the burden of expectation. The first shot across the bow was its world premiere at last month’s New York Film Festival, where Zero debuted alongside prestige fare like Luca Guadagnino’s Sam Altman biopic Artificial and Tony Gilroy’s star-studded Behemoth! There, NYFF’s artistic director Dennis Lim introduced the movie to a sold-out crowd at the Alice Tully Hall, praising Yamazaki for exemplifying "the endless possibilities of creative VFX and genre filmmaking." Minus Zero indeed thrives on spectacle: its opening sequence blazes a merciless path of carnage aided by an elegant long take, while subsequent scenes centered on one of Godzilla’s classic foes, the three-headed Ghidorah, inspire genuine terror more than cheap thrills. This is the first Japanese film shot for IMAX, a large-scale exhibition that’s often torqued for discomfort. Yamazaki’s centerpiece battle pitting the monster against a squadron of fighter planes is dogged by fatalistic doom: a mother and child screaming as their house crashes to the ground don’t get the last-minute salvation we’ve come to expect, and even the sentimental-seeming inclusion of a pilot named Honda is complicated by his eventual fate.

If not quite so grave as the visions of death that imprinted upon a young Kiyoshi Kurosawa, Yamazaki’s narrative—including a face-melting sequence that U.S. distributor GKIDS have asked not be spoiled—provides a stark contrast to the bloodless carnage of American blockbusters. It’s quite the cultural coup, too, that a film this brutal and generally skeptical of American imperialism has secured a simultaneous international release: every English-speaking actor (none recognizable, each portraying arrogant allied military) bears an amusingly off-market quality à la the nefarious white time-travelers of 1991’s altogether underrated Godzilla vs. King Ghidorah.

Nearly all Godzilla films are a total restart. Minus Zero is immediately notable as a direct sequel. The results suggest that Yamazaki overestimated his initial project. Godzilla is not much of a presence in Minus Zero, first appearing around the 50-minute mark and then again in a suitable, albeit brief climax. Far more time is spent with those we came to know and like during Minus One, each reprised by an entirely competent ensemble that fails to elevate interest higher than a certain co-star’s 50 meters. (The protagonists’ adopted daughter from Minus One returns here for the sole purpose of standing in place and crying.) Whatever its pretensions towards grandeur, this is still a film where a scientist explains his master plan by smashing together two monster figures. It takes little to delight in this moment, a literal and figurative collision of serious storytelling and childlike abandon. More of that spirit might’ve served the final picture.

My mild disappointment is nothing compared to the agony Godzilla has wreaked on the district of Ginza, which last week hosted the first public screenings of Minus Zero through the Tokyo International Film Festival. Godzilla’s annihilated the city’s landmarks enough times that when we think of all-out destruction on the sprawling megalopolis that is Tokyo, we’re probably picturing its uber-fashionable shopping sector laid to ruins. When he emerged from the sea in 1954, he wrecked the district’s historic Nichigeki Theater, which was again destroyed (in real life, of humans’ accord) and reopened as the Yurakucho Mullion building in 1984—the same year as The Return of Godzilla, where he inflicted yet more damage on the brand-new structure. Godzilla Minus One recreated the Nichigeki Theater in loving detail only to destroy it again in a sequence that deployed modern visual effects to cause maximum tactility and human misery. That Hiroshima-like site is revisited in Minus Zero, leading one character to declare that “Ginza is again the battleground.” Time’s healed those wounds, however. The night before Minus Zero’s Japanese premiere, a small crowd gathered outside the Yurakucho Mullion’s Seiko watch for an extravagant display: the clock lifted, and out came a small set of Godzilla puppets that strike chimes while Akira Ifukube’s iconic theme plays.

Ginza’s Wako Clock Tower has fared no better: it was torn to ribbons in the 1954 original, 1995’s Godzilla vs. Destoroyah, Shin Godzilla, and Minus One. After a time you must wonder what keeps bringing Godzilla back to the neighborhood. Is it animal instinct, or mere coincidence, or an atomic hatred for its glowing consumerism? The Wako Annex, a nearby pastry shop that Google not-inaccurately describes as “chic,” currently advertises a Christmas-themed cake recreation of the oft-doomed Clock Tower with Minus Zero’s monster looming over it; accompanying text informs us that “Godzilla strikes Ginza’s Wako once again.” The nearby Toho cinema is within Hibiya Godzilla Square, featuring a small but impressively detailed statue and a plaque reading, “The human race must coexist with Godzilla.” Immediately adjacent is a three-story shopping mall hosting a Toho store selling numerous Godzilla ephemera. (I bought the tea cup.)

Even Americans accustomed to the fetishization of disaster would be impressed by Japan’s ability to marry suffering and spectacle to great financial gain. Perhaps it’s the same haunted fascination of a young Martin Scorsese or Kiyoshi Kurosawa cast unto the world at large; Godzilla might be scary as he destroys Ginza, but he’s something to admire when shrunk down to human size and displayed inside the Yurakucho Mullion’s lobby. (The photo-snapping crowds that gather every time I walk past suggest that bit of marketing paid off.) Even as Minus Zero’s first reviews show a less rapturous response than Minus One, this series’ viability—and its newfound prestige—shows little indication of flagging. Ginza’s residents were beyond happy to see Godzilla, at least in ossified, action-figure form. But who's to say they wouldn't be just as excited if, one day, his path of destruction broke through the screen?

#6761. Prince Harry and Prince William Pen Rare Letters About Their Mother to the Winners of the Diana Award

The prize recognizes “young people who work to improve the lives of others”

One area in which Prince Harry and Prince William will always share common ground is in their respect for their late mother, Princess Diana.

Two years after Diana’s untimely passing in 1997, the Diana Award was established by former U.K. Prime Minister Gordon Brown, in an effort to recognize young people who “work to improve the lives of others.” Now, the 2026 recipients have received a special treat in the form of personalized letters from Harry and William, who expressed their congratulations, while recognizing that the winners are helping keep Diana’s legacy alive.

“You should be immensely proud of what you have achieved and the difference you are making in your community and beyond,” Harry wrote in his message. “This award is deeply personal to me, not only because it carries my mother’s name, but because it champions her belief that young people have the power to change the world. You are putting that belief into action and inspiring others in the process.”

Meanwhile, William noted: “The world we live in today can feel challenging and uncertain, and creating change is not easy. Yet, in the face of these challenges, you have shown extraordinary resilience, courage, and a belief in the power of kindness to make things better.”

The Prince of Wales also added: “My mother, in whose memory you receive the Diana Award today, would be so proud of your achievements and the deep care you show for others. Thank you for your compassionate leadership, which is helping to create a more hopeful and positive world.”

Over the past few years, the royal brothers have continued their tradition of honoring Diana Award recipients. Back in 2023, the Duke of Sussex even made an in-person visit to see some of the honorees at a Conversations for Change seminar in Los Angeles.

However, most of their efforts have been done separately, as the two continue to deal with strains in their relationship.

One of the last times the princes were seen together was back in 2021, when they attended the unveiling of a statue dedicated to their mother at the Sunken Garden in Kensington Palace. The ceremony was held on what would have been Diana’s 60th birthday.

#6760. Everything to Know About the 2027 Met Gala: Theme, Hosts and More

As ever, the next Met Gala will celebrate the Costume Institute at the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s spring exhibition. The theme this time? “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday,” examining extraordinary transformations of ordinary garments and materials.

Here’s everything else you need to know about the 2027 Met Gala.

The Met Gala, which provides the Costume Institute’s primary source of funding for all activities, will take place on the first Monday in May: May 3, 2027. The exhibition, which opens to the public on May 9, will be on view through January 9, 2028

Organized by Andrew Bolton, with assistance from Stephanie Kramer and Emily Mushaben, “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday” will approach its subject in two ways: both by looking at how designers have elevated and experimented with simple garments like tees and jeans, and by considering how humble materials like paper, plastic, and metal have been transformed by fashion. “extraORDINARY: fashion and the poetics of the everyday” will be sponsored by Instagram, with major funding from Moncler, and additional support from Condé Nast and Jordan Roth.

The exhibition replaces the John Galliano study originally planned for 2027.

Inaugurating the Met’s new, nearly 12,000-square-foot Condé M. Nast Galleries, the spring 2026 show, “Costume Art,” considers depictions of the dressed body from across the Met’s curatorial departments, pairing garments with art objects spanning some 5,000 years.

Objects in “Costume Art” are divided into a “series of thematic body types,” ranging from the “Naked Body” and the “Classical Body”—both of which are well represented within the museum’s collection—to those, like the “Pregnant Body” and the “Aging Body,” that have more often been overlooked. It remains on view at the Met through January 10, 2027.

Beyoncé, Nicole Kidman, Venus Williams, and Anna Wintour co-chaired the 2026 Met Gala.

Continuing a tradition from years past, the 2026 Met Gala also had a host committee. That group included committee co-chairs Anthony Vaccarello and Zoë Kravitz, along with members Adut Akech, Angela Bassett, Sinéad Burke, Sabrina Carpenter, Doja Cat, Gwendoline Christie, Misty Copeland, Alex Consani, Elizabeth Debicki, Lena Dunham, Paloma Elsesser, Rebecca Hall, LISA, Chloe Malle, Aimee Mullins, Amy Sherald, Tschabalala Self, Sam Smith, Teyana Taylor, Anna Weyant, Lauren Wasser, A’ja Wilson, Chase Sui Wonders, and Yseult. Additionally, as the lead sponsors for the 2026 gala and exhibition, Jeff Bezos and Lauren Sánchez Bezos served as honorary chairs.

The 2026 Met Gala livestream was hosted exclusively by Vogue and broadcast live across its digital platforms, including on YouTube and TikTok. To rewatch it on vogue.com, you can head to this page.

That’s kept mostly under wraps; guests must abide by a no-phone (and, therefore, no social media) policy once they’ve entered the museum. But the run-of-show involves cocktails, dinner, and a high-profile performer—or two. (In 2026, that was Sabrina Carpenter and Stevie Nicks.) Attendees always have a moment to explore the exhibition, too.

Decor is, of course, always taken seriously. For 2026, event designer Raúl Àvila was inspired by the design of Northern Italian gardens, with fruit-forward tablescapes (pomegranates, pears, black wine grapes, artichokes, kumquats) set on striped tablecloths. Check back on what was on the menu for this year’s guests, too.

The Met Gala takes place at The Metropolitan Museum of Art each year. Guests from out of town (and even some based in the city) typically stay at hotels nearby, congregating at a few celebrity-favorite spots. The Mark Hotel is always a prime location for star-spotting; in 2026, the likes of Alysa Liu, Alex Consani, Hudson Williams, Lisa, and Odessa A’zion prepared for their big night out there.

The event usually hosts between 450 and 600 attendees, welcoming stars, young creatives, and paragons from the worlds of fashion, the arts, sports, and politics. 2026 saw a clutch of Met Gala debuts, too: Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams, Chase Infiniti, Paul Anthony Kelly, and Sombr included.
