#6655. Priyanka Mattoo Wants You to Try Leaning Out

It’s no secret that between work, family responsibilities, and the stress of living in a country with little in the way of a social safety net, many Americans—especially mothers—feel maxed out. In 2026, the concept of “doing it all” isn’t heroic or aspirational; it’s simply surviving.

When author Priyanka Mattoo took stock of her busy life in Los Angeles—as a mother of two and the eldest daughter of Kashmiri immigrants—she considered what would happen if she stopped instinctively meeting the needs of everyone around her. The result of that private experiment is her new book How to Be Less Useful: The Joy of Inefficiency, a delightful and useful account of trading compulsive productivity for (gasp) fun. It reads like a gentle yet firm pep talk to stressed-out overachievers everywhere.

Vogue spoke to Mattoo about the lessons she learned from writing her first memoir in 2024, resisting the urge to peel her kids’ oranges, and taking inspiration from Jenny Odell and Nigella Lawson.

Vogue: How did writing this book compare to the process with your first memoir, Bird Milk & Mosquito Bones?

Priyanka Mattoo: I enjoyed it so much more. With the memoir, I felt like I was lancing a boil that had been building for 40 years. I really wanted to write a book for my community and my family, and so the stakes of that, the burden of it, felt really heavy. I had to process a lot of intergenerational trauma for that book to get written the way that I wanted to write it. I was writing about not only a lifetime but generations of lifetimes, because I went back to talking about my grandparents and my great-grandparents. So that was a heavy lift emotionally. This book builds upon the work that I did during the first book, because the process of self-discovery and the therapy that I had to do to get through the first book allowed me to be sort of lighter and gentler with myself. I took two years to write it, but the events of it occur over about a year. What I felt was that in the first book, I processed a lifetime of adverse events, and then in this book, I got to process everything in real time.

What was the hardest part of the beginning of your journey to “be less useful”?

It’s the question of: What’s going to happen if I stop doing everything? Is everything going to fall apart? And you really don’t know until you try it. What I found was that much less fell apart than I thought would. I was clearly working with a very anxious brain and constantly thinking of the worst-case scenario. In the gap that I left, everyone was able to fill most of it. Everyone around me was just like, “Oh, you’re not going to peel my orange? I’ll peel my own orange. That’s fine.”

What do you think some of the biggest structural barriers are to women—mothers in particular—taking time for themselves?

Oh, there are so many systemic problems. I mean, this book only exists because of the patriarchy. I’m describing traditional gender roles that I saw from my own parents, and my parents saw them from their parents. My husband, while incredibly well-meaning, was not conditioned to address domestic duties in the same way that I was. So this is the soup that we’re all coming up in. I say many times in the book that I have immense privilege. Not just financial, but also the time and energy to even think about this stuff. I am an upper-middle-class woman with an expensive education, and those are ways in which I have benefited. Parts of being a working mom are hard even for me, but lots of women are dealing with so much worse. The support that I pay for—a babysitter sometimes, a really good education—I wish everyone had access to that because that, to me, is just the foundation that we should all be handed in a healthy society. I am able to have the life that I have because we make enough money to pay for the things that everyone should have.

How do you redirect the impulse to do things for your kids that they can do themselves?

It’s such a process—first of self-awareness and understanding when you’re jumping in to solve someone else’s problems even when they should do it, and then realizing that your over-functioning causes deficits in other people’s skill development. I’m not just talking about my kids; I’m talking about my parents and my sibling and everyone in my life. I had over-functioned on every front, and once I pulled back and recognized the impulse to jump in and help, which happens to me a thousand times a day, I learned to quiet it and then see what happened. Once I started quieting it, which was very uncomfortable, and waiting to see what happened, which is also very uncomfortable, I was so pleasantly surprised. I learned I had been so arrogant and so controlling that, of course, everyone around me now actually wants to hang out with me instead of that eldest-daughter meme of “Oh God, here she comes.” I still think there’s a little streak of that, but I think I’m much more pleasant to be around.

Everyone I know does too much. It’s just kind of the nature of a coastal, high-achieving milieu, right? When I first handed in the book and we were talking about who I wanted to blurb it, she does so much, so I feel crazy even bringing her up, but as far as an aspirational lifestyle icon: Nigella Lawson.

She was one of them, and then on the other end is Jenny Odell, who wrote How to Do Nothing. I read it right when it came out and was like, I need to start rethinking my relationship to time. That is probably really where the seed for this book started. Nigella and Jenny Odell are both women who do a lot, but they seem to enjoy and appreciate what they’re doing.

This conversation has been edited and condensed.

#6653. Brûléed Kheer (Rice Pudding) With Mango Sorbet

This creamy, always comforting slow-cooked rice pudding is scented with cardamom and sometimes topped with nuts or dried fruit. Versions of it exist across South Asia and beyond, each one slightly different but speaking the same nostalgic language. I’m serving it with a little twist here—a brûléed top for that crackly crème brûlée moment, and a scoop of mango sorbet for brightness and as a nod to the classic sticky rice flavor.

Note: If you are not using a nonstick pot, be extra careful and stir every 4 to 5 minutes; otherwise the rice pudding will definitely stick to the bottom. In the event it does, quickly empty the contents into a new pot and start simmering from low heat again. If you do not have a kitchen blowtorch, you can skip the brûlée. Serve warm or chill for 2 to 4 hours and garnish with saffron threads.

To a medium heavy-bottomed nonstick pot, add 5 cups (1.2 L) whole milk, 1 cup (240 ml) water, one 14-oz. (415 ml) can sweetened condensed milk, 3 green cardamom pods, and one 1" (2.5-cm) cinnamon stick. Bring to a boil and add 1 cup (200 g) jasmine rice or any short‑grain rice, then turn the heat down to low and simmer, stirring often and scraping all the way down to the bottom of the pot to make sure the mixture doesn’t stick or scorch, until the rice is tender and the mixture is thickened, 50 to 60 minutes. Add ¼ tsp. fine sea salt and stir to combine. If the consistency feels too thick add, ¼ cup [60 ml] water and stir to reach your desired consistency.

Scoop the kheer into heatproof serving bowls and top each with 1 to 2 Tbsp. granulated sugar, ensuring the surface is covered completely. Then carefully brûlée using a kitchen blowtorch, moving in a circular pattern, until the sugar is melted and a deep amber color. (You want a thin, smooth crust that shatters when broken.) Top with a scoop of sorbet and serve immediately.

#6651. Turkey Pot Pie

Chicken pot pie is a perfect cozy dinner for chilly fall days, but like most classics, it could use an upgrade. This turkey pot pie is a perfect way to switch up your meal rotation and make sure those Thanksgiving turkey leftovers don’t go to waste. That being said, this dinner is so comforting, it deserves to be made all season long.

What People Are Saying:“This was AMAZING. The filling is delicious, the crust is super flaky and golden brown. I will make this again for sure.” - GoldTeepee

Pop your butter in the freezer for about 15 minutes before you start making the crust so it’s adequately cold. Grab a large food processor and pulse together the flour, sugar, and salt until they’re mixed. Toss in the butter and pulse again until you see pea-sized pieces and larger chunks.

With the motor running, add vinegar and four tablespoons of ice water, one tablespoon at a time, until the dough just comes together and becomes moist. Make sure the dough isn’t wet and sticky or too crumbly (you can test this by squeezing some with your fingers). If the dough is too crumbly and not coming together, add more ice water, 1 teaspoon at a time.

Turn the dough out onto a lightly floured surface and gently squeeze it together. Knead it just a couple of times so it comes together, then split it into two balls. Flatten each one into a smooth disk, wrap them up in plastic, and pop them in the fridge for at least an hour or even overnight if you want to get ahead.

Move your oven rack to the center, then preheat to 375°. Grab a big, deep skillet and melt the butter over medium heat. Toss in the onions and carrots, and stir until they’re soft. Give it about 7 to 8 minutes. Next, add the garlic and cook, stirring, just until it smells amazing (about a minute). Now, grab a spatula or wooden spoon and stir in the flour. Cook, scraping up any tasty bits from the bottom, until the mixture turns golden and starts to bubble—just 2 or 3 minutes.

Pour the wine in slowly, stirring as you go. Let it simmer for about 3 minutes, just until that alcohol smell is gone. Then, slowly add 1 1/3 cups of cream, still scraping up all the good stuff from the bottom. Keep cooking until the mixture starts to boil and thickens up a bit. This should take around 5 minutes.

Fold in the turkey, peas, thyme, and parsley. Give it all a good season with kosher salt and pepper. Take the skillet off the heat and let the filling cool until you’re ready to use it.

Butter up a 9" pie dish or a deep skillet for your crust. On a lightly floured surface, roll out one disk of dough into a circle about 16" across and 1/4" thick. Carefully lay the dough into the pie dish, letting the edges slump down naturally. Trim the dough, leaving roughly a 1" overhang. Finally, pour in the cooled filling.

Roll out the second disk of dough into a 16"-diameter round about 1/4" thick and arrange it on top of the filling. Fold the top overhang into the bottom, pressing firmly to seal. Crimp the edges if you’d like. Using a paring knife, cut slits on top, and brush with the remaining 2 tablespoons of cream and sprinkle with sea salt.

Bake the pie (cover the edges with foil if they start getting too brown) until the crust is golden and the filling is bubbling. This takes about 1 hour 15 minutes. Once it’s done, move the pie to a wire rack and let it cool for about 15 minutes before digging in.

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Cover your pot pie tightly with plastic wrap or store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to five days after baking. If you’d like to make your pot pie ahead of time and freeze it, wrap the whole (baked or unbaked) turkey pot pie tightly in plastic wrap and store in the freezer for up to 2 months.

#6649. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie

This pumpkin pie recipe has converted more than a few pumpkin pie skeptics. It’s the kind of Thanksgiving dessert readers return to year after year—and not just on the holiday. The filling is silky and rich, deftly spiced with cinnamon, ginger, nutmeg, and cloves, and tastes unmistakably of pumpkin.

Sweetened condensed milk and a splash of heavy cream give the custard its velvety texture, while maple syrup and vanilla add depth. We use canned pumpkin purée (Libby’s is our pick) for its consistent texture and concentrated flavor. A blind-baked crust, finished with an egg wash, keeps things crisp underneath all that creamy filling.

The trickiest part is knowing when to stop baking. Look for slightly puffed, set edges and a center that still jiggles gently, like Jell-O. The filling will firm up as the pie cools, giving you smooth, custardy slices. Serve with a generous dollop of whipped cream.

Make it the finale in a classic Thanksgiving feast →

Sure. We tested this very filling in several store-bought pie crusts, with good results. Use an unbaked 9" pie shell and blind-bake it according to the package instructions before adding the filling. Packaged crusts may bake faster than homemade dough, so don’t automatically follow the crust-baking times in this recipe.

Yes. This recipe calls for 2 cups unsweetened pumpkin purée. A standard 15-oz. can contains about 1¾ cups, so you’ll need to open a second can. Save the leftovers for another of our favorite pumpkin purée recipes. And be sure you’re buying plain pumpkin purée, not canned pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices.

Bake the pie up to a day ahead, let it cool completely, then wrap and refrigerate until you’re ready to serve. For longer-term planning, you can freeze the baked pie for up to 3 months.

2 hours (plus 4 hours 30 minutes for chilling)

Preheat oven to 425°. Roll out 1 disk Perfect Pie Crust on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie dish. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes.

Line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Lightly beat 1 large egg, room temperature, in a small bowl just to blend, then brush over inside of crust (not the crimped edges) and continue to bake until crust is set and beginning to lightly brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool.

Do Ahead: Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature.

Preheat oven to 325°. Lightly beat 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, and remaining 2 large eggs, room temperature, in a clean small bowl just to blend. Whisk ⅓ cup (67 g) sugar, 1 tsp. ground cinnamon, ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ½ tsp. ground ginger, ¼ tsp. ground cloves, and ¼ tsp. ground nutmeg in a large bowl until no clumps remain. Add egg mixture, 2 cups unsweetened pumpkin purée, ⅔ cup sweetened condensed milk, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. maple syrup, and 2 tsp. vanilla extract and whisk until smooth. Pour into cooled crust. Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 60–75 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with whipped cream.

Do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature. You can also freeze pumpkin pie up to 3 months in advance.

To a small heatproof bowl, add 1 medium yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, 2 Tbsp. lime juice, 2 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 2 tsp. chaat masala, ½ tsp. cayenne powder, and ½ tsp. fine sea salt.

Remove from the heat and pour the hot oil over the onions. Toss to coat the onions in the spice mixture.

Increase the heat to medium, add 1 medium red or yellow onion (9 oz. [255 g]), finely chopped, cover, and cook until the onion is translucent and beginning to turn brown around the edges, stirring halfway through, about 10 minutes.

Add 1 Tbsp. ground coriander, 1 Tbsp. Kashmiri red chili powder, 1 Tbsp. Garam Masala, 2 tsp. cayenne powder, and 1 tsp. powdered turmeric. Stir to combine and cook until fragrant, about 1 minute. Drain off the excess marinade from the chicken, then add it to the pot along with 3 Tbsp. tomato paste, 1 Tbsp. packed fresh fenugreek leaves, and remaining 1½ tsp. fine sea salt and stir until everything is mixed thoroughly and the chicken is covered with the spices and tomato paste. Remove from the heat and sprinkle with the remaining 1 tsp. Garam Masala, remaining 1 tsp. fresh fenugreek leaves, and cilantro leaves. Serve immediately with lime wedges, Insanely Addictive Pickled Onions, and steamed rice or Indian flatbread.

#6646. For Natural Volume, Wash Your Hair The French Girl Way

We all know that French girls have that special je ne sais quoi (so much so that it’s inspired countless essays on this very site). When it comes to their hair, the style is nonchalant—and yet, somehow also skillfully cultivated. It’s hair that’s air-dries, falls just right, and retains that slightly tousled movement that gives no hint of effort or styling. So how exactly do Jeanne Damas, Brigitte Bardot, Jane Birkin, and more do it?

Hairstylist and French girl herself Daphné Narcy has an idea: It all starts how you wash your hair. “You may be damaging your hair without even realizing it while in the shower,” Narcy says. “When you’re hair is wet, it’s at its most fragile. But habits like washing hair too quickly, scrubbing too hard, or using water that’s too hot may be causing breakage and frizz.”

She offers up eight simple shower-time adjustments to turn your hair into a French girl dream.

The first—and by far the most common—mistake: People wash their hair instead of their scalp. “We rub the lengths against each other, which damages them, and we neglect the roots, where sebum, pollution, and residue accumulate,” says Narcy. Her philosophy can be summed up in one sentence: A healthy scalp is the foundation of healthy hair. It’s also what determines how light the roots feel once the hair is dry.

The heat from a scalding shower lifts the hair cuticle, which can be bad for shine. “The hair loses moisture, becomes more porous and duller, and the color fades faster,” Narcy says. Hot water hurts the scalp, too, making it drier and more irritated. “Water that’s too hot also softens the hair follicles, which can lead to hair loss.” Your new rule of thumb here is disarmingly simple: “If the water feels pleasant on your wrist, without feeling hot, it’s the right temperature for your hair.”

Use your fingertips in small circular motions, without ever scrubbing. “It’s meant to be an invigorating massage, not a scrub,” insists Narcy. It’s also a moment of pleasantness. When you enjoy it, washing your hair becomes a ritual rather than a chore.

If you’ve ever read the back of a shampoo bottle, you know the instructions: Lather, rinse, repeat. And Narcy says that isn’t just to get you to use more product; but instead the double-shampoo is key to keeping hair clean—though only use a walnut-sized amount each time.

“When you use too much shampoo, residue can remain on the scalp, weighing it down, potentially irritating it, and making your hair look dirty faster The result: you end up washing your hair more often, and you get caught in a vicious cycle.”

The lengths should only be lightly touched when it comes to shampooing. “Press your hands together and slide them down, using very light and gentle friction, all the way to the ends. While rinsing, the lather that runs down finishes cleansing the lengths.” Less friction means fewer tangles, less breakage, and mid-lengths that not only stay hydrated but also dry smooth.

#6642. Cranberry Meringue Pie

A big, billowing cloud of meringue tops this crimson beauty and acts as a sweet reprieve from the tart cranberry curd. The vibrant filling is made even more sour with a generous amount of lime juice. Think lemon meringue pie but holiday-ified. Use our Perfect Pie Crust as the base to create a sturdy-flaky foundation, and be sure to start the pie the day before you plan to serve it, as the curd requires several hours of chilling to set into a sliceable texture. Cut into it too soon and it will run onto your plate, creating a messy—albeit delicious—slice.

We never make pie dough without a metal bench scraper. Our favorite is from Gestura. Use the scraper to cut butter, fold dough and nudge it into shape, transfer it from counter to plastic wrap, trim edges, cut strips, and, sure, scrape flour off your counter.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

3 hours (plus 30 minutes for freezing and 5 hours for chilling)

Whisk 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¼ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour and dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more rice flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Let dough disk sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Roll out dough on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1½" overhang. Fold overhang under so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers. Set pan on a rimmed baking sheet and prick bottom and sides of crust with a fork in several places. Freeze, uncovered, at least 30 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 400°. Line crust with a sheet of parchment paper and fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake crust, tenting edges with foil if browning too quickly, until edges are set and look dry, 20–25 minutes. Carefully lift out parchment paper and weights and continue baking crust, gently pressing bottom and sides occasionally with a flat-bottomed measuring cup if puffing up, until bottom looks dry and is golden, 20–25 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let crust cool.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Bring 1 lb. fresh or frozen cranberries, 1½ cups (300 g) granulated sugar, and ¼ cup water to a boil in a large saucepan, then reduce heat to medium and simmer, stirring often, until cranberries soften and burst and most of the liquid has evaporated, 10–15 minutes. Let cranberry mixture cool.

Transfer cranberry mixture to a blender; reserve pan. Add ⅔ cup fresh lime juice and ¼ cup (32 g) cornstarch and blend on high speed until smooth. Scrape purée back into pan (not over heat) and add 3 large eggs, 2 large egg yolks, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Place over medium heat and cook, whisking constantly, until mixture bubbles and thickens to a pudding-like consistency, about 4 minutes. Remove pan from heat. Add ¾ cup (1½ sticks) unsalted butter, room temperature, cut into pieces, and whisk until melted and combined. Strain curd through a fine-mesh sieve, pushing with a rubber spatula, directly into crust. Smooth into an even layer and cover with plastic wrap, pressing directly onto surface. Chill pie at least 4 hours and up to 1 day.

Just before serving, beat 6 large egg whites, room temperature, ¼ tsp. cream of tartar, remaining 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy and sugar is dissolved, about 5 minutes. Increase speed to high and continue to beat until stiff peaks form, about 3 minutes more.

Spoon meringue over filling and swirl decoratively as desired. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue if desired.

#6641. Oven-Roasted Turkey

The perfect Thanksgiving turkey is easier to make than you might think. Whether you're a first-timer planning a Friendsgiving dinner for your closest pals or the one whose house the whole family gathers at year after year, this recipe will help make your turkey the star of the dinner table. Let this be the year you ace Thanksgiving hosting and find your annual go-to guide for everything—roasting time, thawing, the secret to perfectly browned skin—on how to present the perfect roast bird.

Remove the giblets, trussing, and pop-up thermometers from the turkey. Pat the turkey completely dry inside and out with paper towels. If you plan to cut the wishbone out now, face the turkey neck opening toward you and locate the V-shaped wishbone in the neck cavity. With a sharp and flexible boning knife, using a short but firm swiping motion, gently cut the bone from the breast meat by making long incisions on both sides of the bone. Pry the bone loose with a paper towel or clean kitchen towel and discard. Using your fingers, separate the turkey breast from the skin.

In a spice grinder or mortar and pestle, grind all of the spices until they're finely ground and well combined. This will allow the spices to adhere to the surface of the turkey, especially the dried thyme.

Cover the entire turkey with the seasoning mix, turning the turkey over to season the back as well. Be sure to season under the breast skin and in the cavity. Transfer the turkey to a roasting rack. Refrigerate, uncovered, until cold, at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.

Arrange a rack in the lower third of the oven with no rack above it; preheat to 450°. Gently pat the turkey with paper towels to remove any excess moisture. Place the shallot, lemon, garlic, fresh thyme, and sage in the turkey cavity and neck opening. Be sure not to overfill the turkey. Err on the side of not stuffing everything in if it doesn’t fit. The turkey cavity needs airflow to cook evenly, and blocking that airflow will result in a longer cook time and a drier turkey. Drizzle the turkey with oil. Insert a leave-in probe thermometer (if using) into the turkey thigh or breast and transfer the roasting pan to the oven.

Roast the turkey for 30 minutes. Reduce the oven temperature to 350°. Continue to roast until the temperature in the thickest part of the breast registers 155° and the thigh registers 165°, about 1 hour and 30 minutes more, up to 2 hours more, rotating once during cooking to help the skin brown evenly. Let the turkey rest, uncovered, for 45 minutes before carving.

The full list of ingredients and directions can be found in the recipe below.

Store any leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. Leftovers can also be frozen. Chill any carved turkey in the refrigerator until cold, then transfer to a freezer-safe bag or container and label it with the contents and date. Store in the deepest part of the freezer for up to 6 months.

#6640. Simple-Is-Best Stuffing

More than a decade after Victoria Granof introduced this classic Thanksgiving stuffing recipe, it remains a staff and fan favorite. As former test kitchen director Carla Lalli Music puts it, it’s “everything you want about stuffing—straight down the middle.”

The recipe earns its name: buttery bread, sautéed onions and celery, and plenty of fresh herbs, with no unnecessary extras. Irregular, torn pieces of crusty bread create craggy edges that turn golden and crisp, while the broth-and-egg mixture renders the tender, custardy middle. Fresh parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme (sing it with us) bring familiar holiday flavor, backed by a generous amount of butter.

Homemade turkey stock is welcome, but good low-sodium chicken broth from a carton works well. (Or use vegetable broth to make this stuffing vegetarian.) Get the first bake out of the way a day ahead, saving the browning for just before dinner.

Pair it with the rest of our classic Thanksgiving menu →

Choose a sturdy, crusty loaf, such as pane Pugliese, a French white boule, or a country-style sourdough. Skip soft sandwich bread, which can turn mushy once the broth goes in. Weigh out 1 lb. before drying it—the 10-cup measurement is approximate—and don’t skip drying the torn bread in a low oven, even if your loaf is already a day old.

Why bake the stuffing covered, then uncovered?

The covered bake cooks the stuffing through while retaining moisture; the uncovered bake gives you a crisp, golden top. The interior should be tender and cohesive, not dried out. Keep an eye on the stuffing during the second bake rather than assuming it needs the full time. The finished stuffing should be golden and crisp on top and reach 165°F in the center.

Yes. Bake it covered up to three days ahead, until the center reaches 165°F, then let cool briefly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Save the uncovered browning step for serving day. Return the stuffing to a 350°F oven, uncovered, until crisp on top and 165°F in the center, about 45–60 minutes. For longer-term prep, follow our guide to making and freezing stuffing ahead.

What’s the difference between stuffing and dressing?

Stuffing usually refers to a mixture cooked inside a turkey, while dressing is baked separately—but plenty of cooks use the names interchangeably. We prefer versions cooked outside the turkey for the crisp top and edges, but feel free to call it whichever name you grew up using.

Looking for a different take? Try our Sausage-and-Herb Stuffing, Cornbread Dressing With Sausage and Corn Nuts, or any of our other favorite homemade stuffing recipes.

Preheat oven to 250°. Grease a 13x9x2" baking dish with unsalted butter and set aside. Scatter 1 lb. good-quality day-old white bread, torn into 1" pieces (about 10 cups), in a single layer on a rimmed baking sheet. Bake, stirring occasionally, until dried out, about 1 hour. Let cool; transfer to a very large bowl.

Meanwhile, melt ¾ cup unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-high heat; add 2½ cups chopped yellow onions and 1½ cups ¼" slices celery to melted butter. Stir often until just beginning to brown, about 10 minutes. Add to bowl with dried bread; stir in ½ cup chopped flat-leaf parsley, 2 Tbsp. chopped fresh sage, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh rosemary, 1 Tbsp. chopped fresh thyme, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. freshly ground black pepper. Drizzle in 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth and toss gently. Let cool.

Preheat oven to 350°. Whisk 2 large eggs and remaining 1¼ cups low-sodium chicken broth in a small bowl. Add to bread mixture; fold gently until thoroughly combined. Transfer to prepared dish, cover with foil, and bake until an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center of dressing registers 160°, 35–40 minutes.

Uncover dressing; continue to bake until set and top is golden brown and crisp, 35–45 minutes longer.

Do ahead: Dressing can be baked (before browning) 1 day ahead; uncover and let cool, then cover and chill. Uncover and bake until top is golden brown and crisp, 45–60 minutes.

Leftover stuffing? Use it up in our Winter Panzanella With Stuffing Croutons →

#6639. Elf Beauty CEO on Gen Alpha, Record Sales and Cracking the US

After joining a call with Vogue Business, ahead of Elf Beauty’s Q2 earnings, it’s not long before CEO Tarang Amin mentions that this quarter marks the company’s 31st consecutive quarter of net sales growth.

For Q2 2027, net sales rose 51% to $520.8 million, bolstered by retailer and e-commerce channels across the US and the globe. Gross margin grew 160 basis points to 71%, and adjusted EBITDA reached $123.4 million, up 86% year on year. The company, which comprises Elf, Rhode, Naturium and Well People, also updated its guidance for fiscal 2027, predicting net sales of $2 billion, up from $1.9 billion. While the company did not share a financial breakdown by brand, Amin tells Vogue Business that every brand grew. “It was a phenomenal quarter for us,” he says.

Amin assumed his role in 2014, and since 2020, Elf Beauty has acquired Well People, Naturium, and most recently, Rhode (for $1 billion) in a bullish M&A sweep. During the summer, the Elf brand expanded into haircare, launching Elf Hair with a suite of products including a moisturizing shampoo and conditioner, an anti-frizz styling spray, and treatment oil. (Elf’s own brands also include Elf Cosmetics and Elf Skin.)

Amin’s moves could reap a return on investment. According to Euromonitor, the global haircare category is forecast to grow 24% by 2030, reaching £129 billion, while outpacing the growth of established beauty verticals like makeup and fragrance (both in the double digits).

Despite geopolitical uncertainty and inflation softening consumer sentiment, US shoppers are still buying beauty, especially online. This is a win for Elf, as a US-based “masstige” (mass but prestige-positioned) company that took on TikTok Shop before most competitors, and has captured millennial, Gen Z and Gen Alpha shoppers with its affordability, a key concern for shoppers in the US, as we saw with the “blue tsunami” mid-term results this week.

After cracking Gen Z and millennials, Elf Beauty is eyeing up Gen Alpha.

At the same time, Elf Beauty — available online globally — is expanding its retail footprint in a bid to diversify revenue and scale. In fiscal 2025, Elf Beauty took on the Netherlands and Belgium, as well as Poland and Germany through partner Rossmann. The new territories joined the US, UK, Mexico, and Canada, where partners such as Walmart, Target, and Sephora have supported the brand. Then, in September this year, Rhode launched with Sephora in Europe, bringing the brand to more than 500 stores across 19 new markets. Elf Beauty claims that this has boosted quarterly results.

As analysts and beauty retailers take stock, Amin shares his next steps.

CEO Tarang Amin joined the company in 2014.

Vogue: Elf showed strong growth for Q1 2027. What led to this uplift?

Well, we’ve been known for our value proposition for 22 years. And at a time when consumers are more concerned about affordability, our brands shine. It’s not only resonating now, but will continue to resonate as we go forward. I’d say the second thing for us is that we’re in an incredible category where consumers really care about innovation. We’re known for our innovation, taking inspiration from prestige and putting our Elf twist on it, and bringing it [out] at great value. Most important is our unique ability to engage our community. We were one of the first brands on TikTok. We have our own Twitch channel focused on female empowerment. We have the number one branded experience on Roblox. We live with our community, and we give them what they want. It’s made us the number one brand amongst Gen Z, Gen Alpha, and millennials.

Vogue: You mentioned Gen Alpha, which has been a strong cohort for Elf for a while. As consumers, are Gen Alpha similar to, or completely different from, other generations?

We’re seeing more similarities than dissimilarities. They’re digitally savvy consumers, so that [bodes] well [with] us leaning into connected commerce. We’re [a bestseller] on Amazon [and] on TikTok Shop. They are also seeking value. Then also, the way we engage with them is not about selling cosmetics or skincare. It’s engaging with them the way they want to engage. They also care about the values that a company stands for. We are double certified, cruelty-free — by Peta and Leaping Bunny. We are vegan, and we’re the only beauty company that’s Fair Trade certified.

Vogue: How do you intend to grow while maintaining that commitment to quality?

We have tremendous white space. As great as our results have been, only 25% of our business is outside of the US, compared to many at 70%. There’s already pent-up demand for our brands around the world. Sixty-five percent of Elf’s social [following] is outside the US; 75% of Rhode’s social [following] is outside the US. Just a few weeks ago, we launched Rhode with Sephora in Europe, [across] 19 countries. It was Sephora’s biggest launch ever. It beat our launch with Sephora in North America.

The other thing we’re seeing is our brands are highly elastic. Consumers want to see this same prestige quality and incredible prices in other categories. Just a few years ago, we [launched] skincare. Elf Skin is already over a $200 million retail business. And more recently, we entered the haircare category — same concept, where we have a curated six-product line-up, all with very clear frames of reference to prestige [products] but all $10 or under. Just a few weeks ago, we entered the fragrance category with Elf Pop, a line of fragrance and body products. That elasticity of our brands gives us multiple vectors of growth.

Elf Hair launched this year, following the official skincare rollout in 2022.

Vogue: What drew you to haircare, and how did you first notice momentum?

We’ve been hearing hair requests from our community for years. There isn’t a category they don’t want to see Elf in. We have incredible partnerships with our customers around the world. Target is our longest-standing national retail partner in the US. They’re the ones who came to us with Elf Skin, saying, “We think there’s a huge opportunity. You’re the number one brand in face. You should go into skin.” That was a great insight for us. They came to us with Elf Hair as well, saying, “You know, much of the best innovation is actually happening on the prestige side, which isn’t accessible to most consumers.” In the US alone, two-thirds live paycheck to paycheck.

But it’s also a disciplined rollout strategy. I mean, we could probably go to any category we wanted to, but we take our time and really make sure that we’re nurturing these categories. I’m happy that just in the first three months alone at Target, we’re already a top 20 haircare brand with them.

Vogue: Going into the new year, what are your plans for your social media strategy?

I think one of the things that really differentiates us is that we don’t follow a typical beauty playbook in terms of how people go and try to convince people to buy products. We live where our community lives, and we engage them in a way they want to. We just launched our second album. I don’t know another company that is into music, that’s into women’s sports, that has the number one branded experience on Roblox, our own channel on Twitch, and so it’s a much broader view of how we’re engaging with our community. It goes well beyond beauty.

Vogue: Would you ever enter the prestige segment?

For us, accessibility is always going to be one of the hallmarks of the Elf Beauty company. So if you take a look at Elf Color Cosmetics, the average unit retail is about $7 in the US. Elf Skin is about $10. If you look at our Naturium brands, the average unit retail is about $18, and our Rhode brand is about $25. All are incredibly accessible relative to the quality of the products that they deliver. Usually, a similar product would be multiple times higher, and so I’d say accessibility will always be an important element. We can do entry-level prestige as long as it continues to offer great value. I don’t see us going into luxury. I think that’s a different business model. We’re really about democratizing access.

Vogue: You’ve stepped further into Europe. Are you keen to expand in other regions too?

I’d say the whole world is open to us. I mean, just in the last quarter alone, not only did we launch throughout Europe, but our Elf launch in Sephora Brazil was the number one brand that they carry in both dollars and units, which built on the number one position we have with Elf in Mexico. We’re in India with both Nykaa and Amazon, and have a very fast-growing business there. For us, it’s about executing with excellence.

Vogue: We’ve seen the midterm election results come in. How do you feel that will affect your business?

I would say the biggest theme from this election was affordability, and when it comes to affordability, I believe we’re the best positioned of any company — just given our track record. We’re for every eyelid and face, and so long as we continue to deliver that superior value, I feel quite confident about our business.

Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6633. We Tried Every Boxed Stuffing We Could Find—These Are The Only Ones We’d Buy Again

Some mixes taste so homemade, they just might fool your Thanksgiving guests.

In my opinion, stuffing is the crème de la crème of a Thanksgiving feast. I’d choose it over any other carb or veggie side. Everyone knows stuffing balances a buttery, crispy top with a moist, tender interior and subtle aromatics. It should be the greatest complement to a turkey. But sometimes we can’t get around to making a homemade stuffing on Thanksgiving, so we settle for a box mix.

We tried a variety of stuffings so you don’t have to wonder which one to pick up at the grocery store. We were looking for stuffing that could be mistaken for homemade, with a balanced texture and real seasoning. We tried eight stuffings, but only five were worthy of adding to your holiday table or weeknight rotation.

This ShopRite stuffing is super weeknight-friendly, and I wouldn’t hesitate to make this for an easy dinner side. Because it’s made with chicken broth, you can use water to make it without losing too much flavor.

This Pepperidge Farm Stuffing was the most surprising one I tried. Because it contains whole wheat and therefore is a little darker in color, I wasn’t sure I would like it. The flavor was excellent, though, and I really appreciated the homemade feel of having to add your own fresh chopped onion and celery.

It's admittedly been years since I had my end-all, be-all favorite boxed stuffing as a kid, Stovetop’s Savory Herbs. And you know what? It really holds up.

As the name suggests, this boxed stuffing mix is Big-S Savory and loaded with herbs, with a buttery, peppery backbone. It gets perfectly crispy around the edges. It’s both nostalgic-good and delicious enough to keep a box on hand for after Turkey Day, if not just to make these sausage stuffing bites.

Here is where the fooling comes in, with Kinder's Brown Butter & Herbs Stuffing Mix. One bite of this garlicky, nutty stuffing had me say out loud, “Oh, this is deluxe.”

Not only that, but this might be the easiest stuffing of them all, with no fewer than three different ways to prepare and serve it. There’s a sausage-spiked version, a skillet-made version, and an ultra-savory version with leeks. In short, if you're really in the mood for a homemade stuffing experience, but you're running out of prep time, Kinder's stuffing will trick everyone into thinking you made this fully on your own.

While Kinder’s is great when you still want to eat like a Thanksgiving maximalist, some of us want the easiest (but no less delicious) route. In which case, Mrs. Cubbison’s Traditional Stuffing will take you there.

I’ve long been a fan of the brand’s herby, buttery croutons, so I’m not surprised that Mrs. Cubbison’s Traditional Stuffing is yet another one of its products I'll always keep on hand. The bread base is just the right amount of toasted and caramelized, making for a stuffing that's tender and crispy around the edges (no mush here). Plus, it'll even free up some space in your oven since it can be made in the slow cooker, too.

#6632. Starbucks Red Cup Day 2026: Everything to Know to Snag the Freebie

Starbucks Red Cup Day 2026 is just around the corner—but how do customers snag the free reusable cup that’s made this day famous? Let’s take a closer look at the holiday tradition, when it is and how to participate.

Each November since 2018, coffee fans have swarmed Starbucks on Red Cup Day, when the company gives away reusable hot-beverage cups. Customers simply need to purchase a qualifying holiday beverage to get their free cup, while supplies last. Although their drink will be served in a separate cup, coffee lovers can take their collectible cup home, wash it, and keep using it all season long.

In 2026, Starbucks Red Cup Day is Tuesday, Nov. 17. The coffee chain announced the news on its website.

Customers should plan on waking up early to ensure they make it to Starbucks before the free cups run out. They must order a handcrafted holiday beverage—Starbucks will likely share a complete list of qualifying drinks as the date gets closer—and then they will automatically receive a reusable cup.

Starbucks hasn’t officially revealed the design (or designs) for its 16-ounce grande 2026 Red Cup Day cup, as of writing. However, that hasn’t stopped food bloggers and fans from speculating on social media. Some of the top contenders: an argyle design, something botanical and a two-tone red cup.

Will you be up early for Starbucks Red Cup Day? Tell us in the comments below!

#6630. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6629. Condensed Milk Bread Rolls

Recipe by Kallee Krong-McCreery, Escondido, California

These milk bread rolls are enriched with condensed milk, which makes them fluffy and tender with a touch of sweetness.

Baking bread is one of my biggest culinary joys. It feels magical that a handful of pantry ingredients can create a supple dough, which then transforms into tender, browned bread just begging for a slathering of butter. Whether I’m making sourdough French bread or homemade dinner rolls, the process is mostly the same, but a few small ingredient changes can give a recipe a distinct identity. In these condensed milk bread rolls, that small change is a can of sweetened condensed milk.

This recipe was inspired by Brazilian milk buns (pão de leite condensado) and Portuguese sweet bread, which have sweetened condensed milk added to the dough for flavor and a sugary edge. Most of these recipes use a starter technique called tangzhong, where a cooked flour paste is kneaded into the dough to create a fluffy, cloud-like texture similar to that of Japanese milk bread. We simplified the process for our buns, skipping the starter so they come together without advanced planning.

In a small bowl, dissolve the yeast in warm water. In a large bowl, combine the milk, eggs, butter, sugar, vanilla, salt, yeast mixture and 1-1/2 cups of flour. Beat the mixture on medium speed for three minutes until it’s smooth. Stir in enough of the remaining flour to form a soft dough.

Turn the dough onto a floured surface and knead it until it’s smooth and elastic, six to eight minutes. Place the dough in a greased bowl, turning once to grease the top. Cover the bowl and let the dough rise in a warm place until it has doubled in size, about one hour.

Editor’s Tip: When kneading, start with a light dusting of flour, adding more only as needed. It’s normal for dough enriched with eggs and butter to be tacky initially (it eases as you knead and develop gluten), but adding too much flour will make the bread dry.

Punch down the dough. Turn it out onto a lightly floured surface, then divide and shape it into 12 balls. Place the dough balls in a greased 13×9-inch baking pan. Preheat the oven to 350°. Meanwhile, cover the pan with a kitchen towel and let the rolls rise in a warm place until they have almost doubled in size, 45 to 60 minutes longer.

Editor’s Tip: For evenly-sized rolls, divide the dough by weight using a kitchen scale. The best kitchen scales offer measurements in grams and ounces, so you can divvy up the dough easily no matter which system you prefer.

Bake the rolls until they’re lightly browned, 15 to 20 minutes. Cover the pan loosely with foil if the tops brown too quickly.

Since these rolls are yeast-based and require two rises, you have to make them at least a few hours ahead of time, but you can stretch that to the day before. Make the dough as directed, but cover and refrigerate them after shaping and placing them in the baking dish. The next day, let the rolls warm and rise at room temperature before baking them as directed.

You can freeze baked condensed milk bread rolls for up to three months in an airtight, freezer-proof food storage container. Thaw them in the refrigerator, then warm them in a low oven, around 300°, until they’re soft.

Dense or dry rolls are usually the result of underproofing, overbaking or adding too much flour. Proofing gives the yeast time to lift the heavy dough, weaving air into it for a light texture. If the dough doesn’t rise enough, the lack of air produces rolls with a tight, firm crumb. Use the time cues in this recipe as a guide—proofing may take longer in a chilly kitchen, or go faster on a hot day.

Overbaked rolls can be dry or hard because the extended oven time pulls out their moisture. Since ovens vary, set a timer and check them a few minutes early—even three to four extra minutes can make a big difference. They could also be dry if you knead in too much flour, or if you didn’t measure your flour correctly from the start. Extra flour will hydrate as it proofs, sucking up the liquid that would otherwise contribute to tender rolls.

You can tell yeast is active when a creamy, foamy layer forms on the water’s surface a few minutes after mixing it with warm water. It looks like frothy, milky coffee! Although you don’t always have to proof yeast depending on the type and recipe, proofing active dry yeast gives you visual confirmation that it’s viable. Sometimes the yeast can die off even before the expiration date; proofing checks for that. Once the dough is mixed, you’ll see active yeast at work as it starts to expand, rise and relax the dough.

These lightly sweetened rolls are versatile and can be served for breakfast or brunch with your favorite frittata, crispy bacon and a bowl of fruit salad, or with afternoon tea or dinner. The flavor of the condensed milk—especially as it caramelizes on the roll’s tops—would pair especially well with pork chop dinners, which often feature a sweet ingredient. I also want to try them as a twist on croissant ice cream sandwiches in place of the flaky French pastry.

This recipe doesn’t use a whole can of sweetened condensed milk, but don’t toss the rest. Put it to work in other sweetened condensed milk recipes, or try something new and shake up a Vietnamese coffee martini. Better yet, serve condensed milk rolls with the martini for a happy hour to remember.

The promise of AI automation to fix the administrative problems facing universities is a fallacy. These systems will only increase the burdens of already-struggling institutions.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Universities are at a critical point as students and faculty embrace the use of AI. Already, universities like Harvard are introducing courses that feature an AI avatar as an "instructor."

The promises AI offers higher education are familiar: an increase in efficiency as a consequence of less administration, more teaching coverage, better feedback and smarter assessment. But introducing artificial intelligence (AI) systems in an attempt to fix these problems is not the answer. If anything, AI systems will magnify and speed up the bureaucracy that is driving universities' decline.

In practice, the more likely outcome is darker: AI will not simply sweep away the bureaucratic machinery of universities; it will give that machinery a new regime of AI compliance — more policies, more forms, more trackers, more oversight roles and more work downloaded onto faculty who are already stretched thin.

The danger is not that AI will destroy universities but that universities will use AI to preserve the very processes that make them dysfunctional. If this happens, we might see faculty spending less time on research, less time on teaching, and more time on activities that do not directly contribute to the production of knowledge and education of students.

This is already evident in the existing assessment system in the U.K., but shades are creeping into systems elsewhere, providing a window into the future for U.S institutions. A single piece of student work may pass through a plagiarism-detection platform, a grading interface, a moderation spreadsheet for faculty to share feedback, a grade-transfer system, and an exam-board record. Each stage generates its own logins, deadlines, exception rules and audit trails. None of this is inherently malicious. Anonymous marking, moderation, appeals, accessibility and academic integrity are legitimate concerns. But when each concern is implemented as a separate system, the combined effect is administrative incoherence.

In essence, faculty become the human interface between incompatible platforms, spending their time reconciling grades and chasing missing evidence rather than teaching. While this example pertains to U.K. universities, the trend to expand the administrative staff extends to North America. AI simply introduces a new opportunity to increase administration.

AI could, in principle, solve this. It could integrate systems, automate routine reporting, draft feedback, identify inconsistencies and remove duplicate data entry. Yet the institutional incentive is rarely to remove work; it is to make work visible. A university that automates a broken workflow does not necessarily simplify it. It may simply produce faster reports about the broken workflow, more sophisticated dashboards and more elaborate evidence of compliance. The bureaucratic impulse survives by changing its vocabulary: risk management, assurance, transparency, governance, responsible innovation.

At least one possible outcome is that universities will create AI-use policies, require module-level AI statements, mandate disclosure forms, introduce approved-tool lists and establish review committees. Faculty will be asked to redesign assessments, monitor suspected misuse, document their decisions, complete training, and explain their approach to students. Much of this labor will be invisible. It will appear not as a new job title but as an additional expectation attached to teaching.

When something goes wrong, the academic is exposed; when the system works, the institution claims the credit. That asymmetry is corrosive.

That asymmetry is corrosive. It teaches committed staff that careful judgment is not valued as expertise but rather as a compliance risk to be managed, and the consequences will fall unevenly. Experienced faculty, after voicing their concern to no avail, may leave, retire early or disengage. Early-career academics, already precarious because they don't have tenure, will have the least power to resist. Students will receive less of the resource that matters most: sustained intellectual attention.

One possible outcome is that universities will encourage the development of faculty AI avatars and cut hours and employment. The institution will then justify hiring more ‪—‬ not fewer ‪—‬ compliance and "educational enhancement" staff to manage and maintain these AI avatars, negating the idea of efficiency and cost savings. In this scenario, bureaucracy will expand to manage the problems created by its own expansion while undercutting quality for the students who are paying high tuition fees. One might need to hire staff for oversight of these avatars, administrators and lawyers to manage licensing agreements, quality control staff in case things go wrong, and IT teams for integrating them into learning platforms and websites.

There is an alternative to the administrative tasks. AI should be governed by a simple institutional rule: no new compliance requirement without the removal of an equivalent existing burden. If a university requires assessment redesign to accommodate AI, or the introduction of new technology, it should provide protected time, technical support and a single integrated platform. If it expects faculty to manage AI use, it must give them clear institutional backing rather than leaving them to improvise. And critically, it should show how the technology makes work more efficient before rolling it out across the board.

But the deeper issue is not technology but institutional purpose. A university exists — or should exist — to cultivate understanding, judgment and intellectual independence. If its systems consume faculty time, fragment the student experience, and reward documentation over learning, then AI becomes another instrument of managerial self-preservation. The question is not whether universities can adopt AI. It is whether they can resist using AI to automate their own absurdities.

If they cannot, the outcome will be an educational system that looks progressively sophisticated while becoming increasingly hollow ‪—‬ full of monitoring, low on trust; rich in measuring, poor in teaching; obsessed with compliance, indifferent to the people who make education possible; overly procedural sans intellectual life. It will become an audited theater of learning not worth students' time.

Opinion on Live Science gives you insight on the most important issues in science that affect you and the world around you today, written by experts and leading scientists in their field.

Akhil Bhardwaj is an Associate Professor of Strategy and Organization at the University of Bath, UK. He studies extreme events, which range from organizational disasters to radical innovation. Akhil is interested in the epistemological problem of understanding the underlying dynamics that lead up to these events. He also studies how thinking can be improved as well as the implications of AI adoption in the context of strategic management, entrepreneurship, and high-risk systems. His work is philosophically grounded in pragmatism. Prior to joining academia, Akhil has worked as an engineer and manager at CAT., Inc and consulted as a SOX compliance analyst in the U.S.

As a child of the ’90s and lover of all things Christmas, I never really warmed to the minimalist, beige Christmas aesthetic. The ’90s were a time of bold colors and patterns, big lights and collectibles galore. Burgundy, hunter green and gold were the colors of choice, and pops of sparkly silver tinsel adorned many a Christmas tree. Christmas villages sat nestled in fake snow atop mantles or credenzas while animated Santas stood in windows waving their candles. Blow molds adorned porches and homeowners scoured local stores in hopes of snagging a set of popular icicle lights.

Today’s 90s-inspired Christmas decor includes all of the above.  The items on our list are colorful, cheerful and bound to get you in the Christmas spirit.

#6625. Move Over, Bearista: Panera Has New Limited-Edition Snowman Cups For The Holidays

Just when you thought you had enough cute drinkware to last a lifetime.

Starbucks' Bearista cups have already proved that people will go to some pretty extraordinary lengths for an adorable drinking vessel. We're talking painfully early lines, instant sellouts, and resale prices that might make you reconsider how much you really need another piece of glassware.

Now Panera Bread wants in on the fun. Only instead of a cuddly bear, the bakery-cafe is going with another winter favorite, the snowman. And wouldn't you know, there's even a chance to snag one for free.

On December 3, Panera will be giving away its new glass Snowman Cups with qualifying purchases at participating locations. There's one rather important detail, though: Each cafe will have only 12 available for the promotion. Not exactly a generous supply, and something tells me these won't be sitting around collecting dust for very long.

There are two designs to collect, although which one you'll end up with is anyone's guess, as they're packaged in mystery boxes and the reveal comes after you've already gotten your hands on one.

If you're not interested in competing for a freebie, there's another way to get your hands on one. Panera will also sell a limited quantity through its online shop for $25 each, plus tax and shipping.

And if you're making a Panera run anyway, you might as well check out what's new on the holiday menu. The chain is introducing Peppermint White Mocha and Pistachio White Mocha, each available as a latte, iced coffee, or Frozen Java. The iced coffees get sweet cream cold foam, while the lattes and frozen drinks come with whipped cream. You'll also find peppermint bark or pistachio pieces on top, depending on which flavor you choose.

The new drinks and treats are available at Panera locations nationwide starting this week. As for the Snowman Cups, I can't say whether they'll cause the same frenzy as Starbucks' beanie-wearing bear—but I have a feeling those freebies will melt away pretty damn fast.

#6624. Mamdani and Hochul Visit Queens Night Market to Get Out the Vote

Zohran Mamdani wanted to share with the governor, but the vendor at the Taiwanese Yummy tent wasn’t having it. Cheng Liu insisted the New York mayor try his own bowl of beef noodle soup—the chef’s way.

Instead of trying a bite from Governor Kathy Hochul, Mamdani watched and waited as Liu arranged slippery, wide noodles underneath pickled mustard greens, herbs, and slices of succulent brisket that had been cooked for eight hours, all ladled with a delicate broth. Mamdami started to dig in with his chopsticks when Liu rushed over to spoon in a generous amount of homemade chili oil.

“The mayor is not scared of spicy food,” Liu said via his son’s translation. “We wanted to give him Taiwanese cuisine.”

At the Queens Night Market, Mamdani and Hochul struck an unusual pair: a New York mayor and governor who get along.

Three days before Election Day, the political allies arrived at Flushing Meadows Corona Park in a motorcade of black SUVs to pose for photos and get out the vote for the Democratic party. Hochul has made the city part of her final push in a reelection campaign against Republican Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive endorsed by President Donald Trump.

In a joint interview with Hochul, Mamdani told Bon Appétit that he was showing up for the governor because she was showing up for immigrant New Yorkers. Earlier this year, Hochul signed legislation to ban local and state law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration operations, and to stop police at all levels from covering their face when interacting with the public.

“The governor has stood up and called for public safety to actually be public safety and not just be an assistance and an accompaniment of ICE,” Mamdani said. “That has been part of what makes people feel like they can be part of this city.”

The mayor also mentioned that the Queens Night Market was a favorite with constituents because of the price. Every dish is capped at $6. Hochul, running on affordability, points to her expansion of free school lunch statewide. “As a mom, this is personal,” she said. “I made a lot of peanut butter and jelly sandwiches over the years for kids.”

Representing different generations and factions of their party, Mamdani and Hochul recognize what they stand to gain together. Mamdani needed Hochul to expand free childcare and greenlight plans for a second-home tax. Hochul needs the enthusiasm of the Democratic Socialist mayor’s voting bloc.

Hochul said she and Mamdani are aligned on lowering the cost of living and supporting the small business owners that make the food and nightlife scene so special.

“It’s a rare day in New York for this kind of relationship,” Hochul said, “but when we talk to each other, we don’t disagree on these issues.”

The pair of politicians approached the night market in a coordinated operation that included advance teams, extra security, and business casual ’fits: Hochul in jeans, Mamdani tie-less in a quarter-zip. The mayor—who has made his appetite a key part of his public identity—appeared less stiff in his interactions with food vendors, but Hochul gamely grabbed chopsticks and posed for selfies.

John Wang, who launched the Queens Night Market in 2015, said politicians are a regular presence here. “Every election season, they come out,” Wang said. “Even if they’ve never been here before, they’re like, ‘Yeahhh! I love the Queens Night Market.’” He said some (2020 presidential candidate Andrew Yang, for instance) get feted like Mamdani, and others (N.Y. Sen. Chuck Schumer) draw a tamer response. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez used to come a lot, Wang said, and would always get swarmed by supporters.

For the last market of the season, which fell on Halloween, Mamdani might as well have been a member of BTS. Vendors and visitors alike stared slackjawed, squealed, and uttered “oh my God!”

A young man named Asad showed up in a Mamdani costume with no idea he would meet the mayor, let alone pose for photos that brought him to tears.“This is Bruce Blakeman’s nightmare!” the mayor said of his Mamdani double.

“It was surreal, emotional a little bit,” said Asad, who declined to share his last name. Asad said he was born in Karachi, Pakistan, became a U.S. citizen in 2022, and voted for Mamdani after moving to New York from Florida.

At the Ella Spice stand, Akera Phillip represents Grenada with breadfruit croquettes, fried cou-cou, and to-go pouches of sorrel. Phillip, who named her business after her grandmother, felt “elated” and “blessed” to serve her food to the leaders of the state and the city.

“As a small island girl, it just made me feel big,” she said.

Akera Phillip holds breadfruit croquettes.

At the Epis by Steve tent, Hochul told Steve Lahens she could handle “Buffalo spicy,” a nod to her hometown, rather than admit to any trouble with his Haitian pikliz. Lahens and his wife fixed up plates of griot (fried pork) with diri djondjon (black rice) and makawoni au graten, a Caribbean mac and cheese he makes with bell peppers, “evaporated milk and a few little things I can’t talk about.”

Lahens said he was born in Haiti but came to the U.S. in 1988. A workplace injury pushed him toward cooking, “and it changed my life, for the better.” He began cooking out of his house but now works out of the Mangrove shared kitchen at the Flatbush Central Caribbean Marketplace. He was excited to hobnob with the governor and the mayor, but Lahens also said New York small businesses need more help.

“The rent could be lower so people like me could get a spot,” Lahens said. “Right now I’m stuck in catering. I love it, too, but my whole plan and goal is to get a storefront.”

#6623. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6622. Popeye’s Is Bringing Back This Side Dish for the First Time Since the ’90s

Popeyes is bringing back a nostalgic side dish on Nov. 2, and fans will have plenty to celebrate.

There are two kinds of people in this world: those who go to Popeyes for the chicken and those who will make a special visit just to eat the Cajun fries. Personally, I’m in the second camp. Granted, I have nothing against Popeyes chicken! But the Cajun fries are so deliciously seasoned and perfectly crispy that sometimes I will drive-thru and get them as a snack.

And if you’re also a fan of Popeyes’ side dishes, I have some particularly good news. The Louisiana chicken chain is reaching into its menu archives to bring back a nostalgic favorite that hasn’t been widely available since the ’90s. Let’s just say your next Popeyes order might look a little different!

Popeyes has a long history of serving up more than just fried chicken. When the chain first opened in 1976, its menu featured everything from fried clams to chicken liver. Among those early offerings was a beloved side that eventually disappeared from menus in most markets. But it’s about to make its triumphant return because Popeyes is bringing back Cajun Onion Rings!

The hand-sliced, hand-battered onion rings were slathered with Cajun seasoning. With a distinctive crispy bite, they became a fan favorite almost immediately. In fact, I have family members who constantly compare other fast-food onion ring offerings to the Popeyes version they remember from childhood. In their memories, the Popeyes onion rings were always better!

But the onion rings slowly disappeared from menus. Some locations served them until the 1990s, but by then it was mostly a thing of the past. Now, nearly three decades later, the side dish is finally making its way back.

Onion rings are officially back on the Popeyes lineup now. Availability may vary by location, but this is when you should expect to see them on menus at your local Popeyes.

Priced at $3.99, the Cajun Onion Rings are designed for sharing, although I certainly wouldn’t blame anyone for keeping the whole order to themselves. After all, crispy onion rings are pretty hard to resist. I might even order the onion rings and fries and mix ’em together.

Will you be ordering the new Cajun Onion Rings? Let us know in the comments below!
